articles.title: Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
articles.summary: Scientists say the developing El Niño is now the strongest on record with weather impacts already being felt around the world.

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolou/Getty Images
Wildfires fuelled by El Niño are affecting around 12.5 million people across Indonesia, according to the country's health ministry.
ByBen RichLead Weather Presenter and Simon King Lead Weather Presenter
The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures.

Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015.
Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year.
El Niño can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt.
What is El Niño and how is it measured?
El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year.
Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards.
Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world.
Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared.
There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however.
The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average.
This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI).
Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI).
This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change.
By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks.
Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event.
"The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño."
Impacts of El Niño already being felt globally
Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed.
And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather.
Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide."
El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others.
Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather?
El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data.
Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal.
Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere.
So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began.

Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia.
These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe.

blocks.caption: Map of typical effects of El Niño episodes on precipitation patterns for each region. Key trends are drying in many equatorial regions (northern South America, central Africa, South East Asia and Australia), marked in brown. Southern United States generally becomes wetter than normal, marked in g…

blocks.text: Will there be an impact on UK weather?
The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions.
However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter.
A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December.
The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record.
In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm.
As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.

Son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and entrepreneur Rande Gerber died at a rehabilitation facility

The

blocks.text: The death on Sunday of Presley Gerber, the 27-year-old son of supermodel Cindy Crawford and entrepreneur Rande Gerber, is being investigated as a suspected overdose, according to police.

Gerber died at a rehabilitation facility, Los Angeles county medical examiner records show. An autopsy was performed, but more testing was required before investigators could give a cause of death for Gerber, which the medical examiner did not immediately do.
A news release issued later by the Santa Monica police department then said the agency was investigating his death as a suspected overdose.

Presley, who was his parents’ eldest child and brother of model Kaia Gerber, had spoken often of his mental health and long-term addiction struggles. On the podcast Studio 22 in 2023, he said he hoped sharing details about his struggles would help others coping with mental health difficulties.

“That’s really what I want to do: help people, whether you’re depressed, you’re struggling with something that is having a negative effect on your body,” Presley said. “I mean it could be anything, and there’s no judgment.”

His death was first confirmed by Allie Jenkins, a representative for Crawford and Rande Gerber. “The family is asking for privacy during this very difficult and painful time,” Jenkins said in an email.

Born in California in 1999, Presley was signed by IMG Models at age 15, making his runway debut in 2016 for Moschino’s Resort show in Los Angeles. He worked with brands including Celine, Calvin Klein, Dolce & Gabbana and Pepsi.

articles.title: After floods, Nepal minister demands 'climate justice'
articles.summary: With Nepal still reeling from the devastating floods in August, Kathmandu is calling for climate justice and seeking compensation from the UN-backed Loss and Damage Fund, Environment Minister Geeta…

image.caption: Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhry (r) said Nepal will 'no longer negotiate on vague promises' as the climate crisis escalatesImage: Shalu Yadav/DW

blocks.text: Nepal is seeking $20 million (just under €17.5 million) from the international Loss and Damage Fund, the UN-backed mechanism designed to support countries suffering irreversible climate-related losses, Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary said in an exclusive DW interview.
The move comes after floods and landslides killed more than 1,400 people in August and left thousands missing.
"We have already issued the official letter for the fund for the loss and damage," Chaudhary told DW. "Most of the countries have sent us a positive response."

The flash flooding caused widespread destruction across large swathes of Nepal, damaging homes, agricultural land and infrastructure. Rescue and recovery efforts are still ongoing in several areas, while authorities continue to assess the full scale of the losses.

In the Himalayan nation, the tragedy has become a powerful symbol of what developing countries describe as the unfair climate burden of contributing little to global emissions while facing disproportionate consequences.
'Sympathy alone will not work for us'
Talking to DW, Chaudhary repeatedly framed Nepal's response through the lens of climate justice, a concept that has become increasingly prominent in global climate negotiations.
"Sympathy alone will not work for us," she said. "We don't need sympathy. We need justice. It's high time. If you're not able to give us justice, then we also don't need the words."
"Those countries who are emitting the most and are able to contribute the funds, they need to pay for the climatic disasters like what we are facing," she said.

Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Its geography, however, makes it extremely vulnerable to climate-related risks. Rising temperatures in the Himalayas have accelerated glacial retreat and increased concerns about glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and extreme weather events across the region.
Alps warming fast: Europe's water lifeline is running dry

In the wake of the most recent disaster, the government has intensified calls for more adaptation financing, direct access to climate funds and stronger international commitments to fight consequences of climate change.
'The world is watching'
Chaudhary pointed to melting glaciers, warming temperatures and changes in mountain environments as factors behind the deadly floods.
"Our evidence is showing that this catastrophic event is because of climate change," Chaudhary said.

While many scientists agree that climate change increases the likelihood and severity of such events, establishing a causal relationship between a specific disaster and global warming typically requires detailed attribution studies.
Researchers are more likely to point to a combination of factors, including glacier and permafrost degradation, extreme weather conditions and geological vulnerabilities.
The Nepali government, however, insists that the connection is clear.
"We are the real example and the world is watching us," Chaudhary told DW.
Building support ahead of COP31
The minister's comments come as Nepal seeks to build momentum for COP31, the UN's annual climate conference set to be held in Turkey this November.
When asked about her government's plans for the conference, Chaudhary said "Nepal will no longer negotiate on vague promises or slow-moving traditional and development aid."

According to the minister, Nepal intends to push for greater recognition of the specific challenges facing mountainous countries, arguing that global climate discussions often overlook the risks confronting Himalayan regions.
"Mountain issues need to be addressed," she said. "The world needs to see us, that we are victimized countries. We are paying the price."
Chaudhary also pointed out that Nepal received strong backing from fellow vulnerable nations at the recent gathering of Least Developed Countries (LDCs) in Timor-Leste.
"All the LDCs stood with us," she said. "They are very concerned."
The government plans to bring climate concerns to the UN General Assembly, highlighting the recent disaster and calling for concrete support from the international community.
Nepal to improve its early warning systems
The scale of the disaster has also prompted scrutiny inside Nepal, particularly of the country's warning systems and its disaster response.
Residents in some affected areas have complained that warnings came too late or did not adequately reflect the scale of the danger.
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes
Chaudhary defended the government's response but conceded that existing systems were overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the event.
"We had sent them messages and information," she said. "But the situation was beyond imagination."
She acknowledged that Nepal's early warning systems must improve and said authorities are now reviewing and strengthening existing monitoring mechanisms.
"Our hydrology and meteorology departments are working on that," she said.
The floods also highlighted the importance of cooperation between Nepal and its neighbors, particularly China, in monitoring river systems and glacial hazards that cut through national borders.
"We are working closely," Chaudhary said, adding that technical teams from both countries are sharing information and examining future risks.
Himalayan catastrophe as a warning for the world
For Chaudhary, the disaster is not only a national tragedy but a warning about the future.
"Our snow is melting, our lakes are in danger," the minister said.
She warned that, unless global warming is limited in line with the Paris climate agreement of 2015, vulnerable countries could face increasingly severe disasters.
Asked whether the world is acting fast enough, the minister responded: "I don't think so."

blocks.text: Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.
Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.
The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest attack in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.

All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the attack on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.
The accused had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms.

items: Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte is expected to testify in the impeachment trial of his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, from September 28 to 30, 2026, as per a subpoena delivered to his office.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate impeachment court on Tuesday, September 22, said it expected Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte to participate in the impeachment trial of his older sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, next week.
Impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol confirmed that the Senate sergeant-at-arms had delivered the subpoena ad testificandum et duces tecum to the mayor’s office in Davao City.
Under the subpoena, Baste was directed to appear before the impeachment court from September 28 to 30, 2026.

He was also ordered to produce certified true copies of relevant official records in the custody of the Davao City government, including “all contracts and similar transaction records entered into from 2020 to the present with: Gencorp Industries Inc.; and any corporation or other entity that owns or operates a Jollibee branch or establishment.”

“We’re expecting that all witnesses, not only Mayor Duterte, will adhere [to] the court’s compulsory process and that they will be present here for the impeachment trial next week,” Tongol said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Gencorp Industries was linked to the Vice President after she declared in her 2022, 2023, and 2024 Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she was a stockholder of the company.
However, Sara’s name did not appear as an incorporator or stockholder in Gencorp’s corporate records, according to Securities and Exchange Commission Director Gerardo del Rosario.
Baste, in a statement, also denied that Sara’s name or even the Duterte surname appeared in any of the company’s official documents submitted to the Davao City government.
He said Gencorp had secured 19 contracts worth P33 million with the city government since 2022, a figure higher than what Rappler initially reported.
“I, and all other officials and employees of the City Government of Davao, never had any knowledge of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte holding an interest in Gencorp Industries Inc.,” he said.

“Furthermore, neither the name Sara Zimmerman Duterte nor the surname ‘Duterte’ appears in any of the official documents such as, among others, the Articles of Incorporation, submitted by Gencorp Industries Inc. across the 19 contracts and transactions in question,” he added.

The impeachment court had initially directed the mayor to appear at the trial on Wednesday, September 23. However, it recalled the subpoena and reset his appearance in view of the oral arguments on the voting threshold.

Senator-judge Bam Aquino, in an interjection during Tuesday’s hearing, asked the defense counsel about Duterte’s role in the company, noting that the Vice President herself had declared Gencorp in her SALN.
Defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular said it would be premature for the defense to answer the question.

“I was expecting that answer, but like what the amicus curiae said, at the end of the day, the impeachment trial is sui generis, and we can follow our own path towards truth and fairness,” Aquino said, adding that Gencorp officials may shed light on the Vice President’s position in the company.
Del Rosario identified Kimberly Justine Y. Cruz as Gencorp’s president, Richie Yvette L. Cruz as treasurer, and Girley S. De La Cruz as corporate secretary.
Meanwhile, Del Rosario said Duterte should have known to divest from her business interests upon assuming the vice presidency in 2022.

“The law is clear that there is a prohibition, and she should have known that as a high-ranking government official. When she took her oath as Vice President, she swore to act within those limitations. So, ideally, before she took her oath, she should have removed herself from it or divested,” Del Rosario said.

Article VII, Section 13 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the President, Vice President, Cabinet members, and their deputies or assistants “shall not, unless otherwise provided in this Constitution, hold any other office or employment during their tenure.”

It also states that they “shall not, during said tenure, directly or indirectly, practice any other profession, participate in any business, or be financially interested in any contract with, or in any franchise, or special privilege granted by the Government,” and that they “shall strictly avoid conflict of interest in the conduct of their office.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Kansas judge reportedly convicts driver in death of teacher whose husband was killed months prior
articles.summary:
Ashleigh Boyd died in a car crash months after Adan Manzano, a TV reporter, was killed in Louisiana while preparing to cover the Super Bowl

A Kansas school teacher’s fatal car wreck on…

blocks.text: A Kansas school teacher’s fatal car wreck on Monday reportedly led to a vehicular homicide conviction for the motorist who crashed into her – a verdict delivered just four days after a Louisiana jury found a woman guilty of the drugging death of the educator’s widower while he prepared to cover the 2025 Super Bowl for Telemundo.

Todd W Armstrong’s one-day bench trial in an 11 April 2024 traffic collision that killed Ashleigh Boyd in Topeka, Kansas, resulted in the judge, Andrew Holmes, finding him guilty of vehicular homicide, according to the victim’s father, Brian Hinck. Armstrong, who had pleaded not guilty, was tentatively scheduled for sentencing in November, Hinck said.

Hinck did not immediately describe a reaction to Armstrong’s guilty verdict. Neither the office of the Topeka district attorney, Mike Kagay, nor Armstrong’s lawyer could immediately be reached for comment late on Monday.

Beforehand, Hinck had publicly discussed how much he loathed the idea of Armstrong’s trial happening so soon after the conclusion of a separate one centering on the unrelated, 5 February 2025 death in suburban New Orleans of his son-in-law, Adan Manzano.

Hinck said he and his wife, Nicole, are raising Boyd and Manzano’s daughter, three-year-old Eleanor, after her parents’ deaths 10 months apart. And he had said it was also bitterly disheartening for him to learn that Armstrong, 55, faced no more than one year in prison even if found guilty of vehicular homicide because Kansas law considers the offense a misdemeanor.

Hinck furthermore said he was incredulous that the woman at whose hands Manzano died, according to the Louisiana jury, was on probation at the time of the crime – and that the cases strained his faith in parts of the US criminal justice system.
“The disappointment in the justice system is at a peak level in our house,” Hinck had said.

Boyd, 24, was in her sedan when Armstrong – in a pickup truck on the wrong side of the road – hit her head-on. The teacher at Topeka’s Lowman Hill elementary school was pronounced dead at the scene, and Eleanor – then an infant passenger – was injured, according to investigators.

Court records cited by the Topeka news station KSNT alleged that investigators recovered evidence showing Armstrong’s truck had been parked for five hours at a casino in Kansas City, about an hour’s drive away, on the morning of the crash. Armstrong allegedly told authorities that either a blown tire or mechanical failure caused him to crash into Boyd, though investigators detected no obvious signs of such defects in his truck, said the court records reported by KSNT.

There also evidently was a urine drug screen result indicating the presence of cocaine metabolites in Armstrong’s system, as the Topeka Capital-Journal reported. However, according to court records, Armstrong’s attorney successfully argued that the drug screen result should be omitted from being considered as evidence during the defendant’s trial.

Meanwhile, Boyd’s husband, Manzano, was working for the Spanish-language Telemundo affiliate in Kansas City when he traveled to cover Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans. Manzano was found dead in his hotel room in the New Orleans suburb of Kenner, Louisiana, days before one of the teams he covered – the Kansas City Chiefs – played in the big game.

Investigators ultimately determined Manzano had been preyed on by a group who descended on victims in New Orleans’ French Quarter, knocked them unconscious by furtively drugging them, and stole their phones and bank cards to drain their financial accounts.
Manzano’s autopsy revealed the native of Toluca, Mexico, had died lying face down on a pillow, having asphyxiated after ingesting a combination of alcohol and the pharmaceutical depressant Xanax.

On Thursday, after a four-day trial, a jury at a suburban New Orleans state courthouse convicted Danette Colbert, 49, of negligent homicide in Manzano’s death. That jury also convicted both Colbert and her accomplice, Rickey White, 35, of racketeering.

A third defendant in Manzano’s death, 35-year-old Christian Anderson, ultimately testified against Colbert and White, whose sentencing was tentatively scheduled for 28 September. Anderson pleaded guilty to lesser charges of simple robbery and fraud in exchange for a six-year prison sentence.
Negligent homicide can carry up to 10 years in prison. Racketeering can carry up to 50 years’ imprisonment.

Separately, after Manzano’s death but before her trial, Colbert received a 25-year prison sentence for violating her probation on a prior theft and fraud conviction and being classified a habitual offender.
Hinck spoke in between the Colbert–White and Armstrong trials about battling to shield Eleanor from the particulars of the legal fallout surrounding her parents’ death.
“We don’t talk about it with her,” Hinck said in reference to his granddaughter. “The only thing she knows is her mom and dad are in heaven, and she will see them one day.”

articles.title: Jenna Timmons-Oikawa wins 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize
articles.summary: Ottawa-based writer Jenna Timmons-Oikawa has won the 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize for her story Wawa Indian, inspired by themes of reclamation and renewal.

image.caption: Jenna Timmons-Oikawa is a writer based in Ottawa. (Shanon Oikawa)

blocks.text: CBC Literary Prizes
Ottawa-based writer Jenna Timmons-Oikawa has won the 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize for her story Wawa Indian, inspired by themes of reclamation and renewal.
Ottawa-based writer wins $6,000 and 2-week writing residency in Banff, Alta.
· CBC Books
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 8:15 AM EDT | Last Updated: 33 minutes ago
Ottawa-based writer Jenna Timmons-Oikawa has won the 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize for her story Wawa Indian.
She will receive $6,000 from the Canada Council for the Arts and a two-week residency in the Leighton Artist Studios at Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity.
Timmons-Oikawa's non-fiction piece was published on CBC Books. You can read Wawa Indian here.
This year's finalists were selected by a jury composed of Claire Cameron, Niigaan Sinclair and Teresa Wong.

"Wawa Indian was a real pleasure to read and a refreshing narrative that took the jury on a dynamic journey. The story is a metaphorical, time-shifting and complicated exploration of identity, contradiction and 'living through history.' At the same time, the narrator's voice is generous and empathic, representing the tenderness of growing up and the tragedy of truth," the jury said in a statement.
"Bringing together past and present, Wawa Indian plays with language, illustrates the complexity of humanity and offers hope to a world built on harm and cynicism."

Timmons-Oikawa told CBC Books that Wawa Indian was inspired by themes of reclamation and renewal. Reclaiming stolen heritage and culture has been an often confusing and sometimes messy human experience, she said.
"It is something that I have been and will be working toward for the rest of my life."
Writing this piece brought to light some feelings I had been holding on to, and brought to my consciousness many things I had been not allowing myself to believe- Jenna Timmons-Oikawa

"It wasn't until last year, when I wrote this piece, that I fully came to terms with, and emotionally understood that, my mom was taken. She wasn't just a gift given to my grandparents, but a stolen person," said Timmons-Oikawa.

"Though I had researched the Sixties Scoop and logically knew what had happened, it still had felt emotionally disconnected from me," she said. "Writing this piece brought to light some feelings I had been holding on to — and brought to my consciousness many things I had been not allowing myself to believe."

items: Read Wawa Indian by Jenna Timmons-Oikawa

blocks.text: Timmons-Oikawa lives on the traditional, unceded territory of the Anishinaabe Algonquin Nation in Ottawa. Her work has appeared or is forthcoming in The Malahat Review, The Fiddlehead and PRISM International, and she was selected as first runner-up for Canadian prose as part of The Temz Review's inaugural "London" Literary Prizes.
She holds a bachelor of arts in creative writing, a diploma in child and youth counselling and spent a decade working with youth in the mental health field.
Timmons-Oikawa joins a long list of writers who have won CBC Literary Prizes, including Lorna Crozier, David Bergen, Michael Ondaatje and Carol Shields.

items: Claire Cameron, Niigaan Sinclair and Teresa Wong to judge 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize
Famous Canadian writers who won CBC Literary Prizes

blocks.text: The CBC Literary Prizes have been recognizing Canadian writers since 1979.

“To have [the judges] select this piece as the winner of the CBC Nonfiction Prize is truly a privilege. I can't thank CBC, the readers and the judges enough for seeing the value and beauty in my story. It was transformative for me to write, and to have it read and honoured in this way by three distinguished Canadian non-fiction writers, is transformative as well. Not enough people get to live out their childhood dreams, and now I am a lucky one of the few."
It was transformative for me to write, and to have it read and honoured in this way by three distinguished Canadian nonfiction writers, is transformative as well.- Jenna Timmons-Oikawa
The other four prize finalists were:

items: Brendan Bowles, of Toronto, for I Told You This Would Be Beautiful.
Lana Hall, of Toronto, for Last night at the Blue Ridge Inn.
Kristina Kasparian, of Montreal, for Bad Faith.
Jacky Sawatzky, of Lanark Highlands, Ont., for Radiation Nights: Voice memos to a friend.

blocks.text: They will each receive $1,000 from the Canada Council for the Arts.
The longlist was selected from more than 1,900 submissions, which are processed by a two-tiered system.
Initial submissions are screened by a reading committee chosen for each category from a group of qualified editors and writers across the country. Each entry is read by two readers.

The readers come up with a preliminary list of approximately 100 submissions that are then forwarded to a second reading committee. It is this committee who decides the approximately 30 entries selected for the longlist, which is forwarded to the jury.

items: Meet the 2026 CBC Nonfiction Prize readers

blocks.text: Works are judged anonymously on the basis of the participant's use of language, originality of subject and writing style. For more on how the judging for the CBC Literary Prizes works, visit the FAQ page.
Last year's winner was Laura MacGregor for her story The Invisible Woman.
The 2026 winner of the Prix du récit Radio-Canada is Raphaël Potvin for Points de suture.

If you're interested in other writing competitions, check out the CBC Literary Prizes. The 2027 CBC Short Story Prize is currently accepting submissions. The 2027 CBC Nonfiction Prize will open in January and the 2027 CBC Poetry Prize will open in April.

articles.title: Could we see MMA at the Olympics?
articles.summary: Mixed martial arts has made its debut at the Asian Games this week. It takes the sport closer to the Olympics but there are doubts about the next step, and the influence of the popular and lucrative…

image.caption: MMA has made its debut at the 2026 Asian GamesImage: Dita Alangkara/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The form of mixed martial arts (MMA) making its debut at the Asian Games looks almost completely distinct from the visceral brawls of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), which have come to define combat sports in recent years.

In order to get a version of the sport into the Games, currently taking place in Nagoya in Japan, adaptations had to be made. The fights take place without the familiar cage, on an open mat and with small boxing-style gloves. While MMA's presence in the Asian Games is significant in itself, it's also a clear effort to get close to Olympic recognition.

"We think without the cage we will have a better alignment with the Olympic values and hopefully recognition from the IOC," Galastein Tan, the director general of Federation of International Mixed Martial Arts (FIMMA), told press agency AP. "It takes time to change a perception. We hope to be able to share that there is a new form of MMA, and this form is more aligned with the Olympics."

FIMMA is not the only body purporting to represent the sport, with the International Mixed Martial Arts (IMMAF) also staking a claim. But Tan, a Chinese billionaire property mogul, is a vice president of the Olympic Council of Asia. This could potentially open doors in a movement which has so far kept MMA at arm's length, with violence levels among its concerns. DW contacted both FIMMA and the IMMAF for comment but received no response.
UFC has outstripped MMA

In the past the UFC, a lucrative MMA-based competition, has also pushed for Olympic recognition. But the growth of that arm of the sport, highlighted by it staging an event on the South Lawn of the White House at the 250th anniversary celebrations of US independence earlier this year, has meant that the aims of a sport that was marginal two decades ago have shifted according to Karim Zidan.

blocks.caption: UFC hosted matches at the White House earlier this yearImage: Kent Nishimura/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I don't necessarily think it's that important to MMA. The sport has already found its success on a professional level, which is what the fan base demanded of it," said Zidan, who has written an upcoming book 'The Ultimate Strongmen: MMA and the Rise of the New Authoritarian Right' on the subject.

"The UFC is bigger than it's ever been in terms of the amount of money it's making" added Zidan. "The UFC's growth mainstreamed MMA as a sport, but it also cannibalized it. So there's really not much remaining. Olympic recognition might seem like a badge of honor, but it doesn't amount to much else."

With events for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles already set, the earliest MMA could make its bow would be 2032 in Brisbane. But the IOC told AP that "mixed martial arts does not meet ... eligibility criteria" at this point. DW has sought clarification from the IOC on this.
Does MMA have enough appeal for Olympics?
Tan appears to be trying to find a way to change that, citing the sport's popularity. "MMA is popular globally, able to engage fans at a gut level and attract fans at a youth level," he said.
But Zidan argues that its popularity is through the UFC, rather than any grassroots popularity.

"There isn't much of an MMA ecosystem outside of the UFC for me to say there's an entirely different worldview existing in the sport that's demanding this. There are pockets within the sport that enjoy amateur MMA and are operating within it, but I don't think it's a significant part of the fan base at all," Zidan said.

"I'm not particularly convinced that this is a turning point or a significant moment for mixed martial arts, honestly. I think the sport has suffered tremendously under the burden and the weight of the UFC over the past decade."
Senegal gears up for Youth Olympic Games
UFC's links with the Trump administration are deep and clear, with UFC president Dana White also speaking at the Republican convention in 2024.

But Zidan also pointed to the IMMAF's link up with Brave Combat Federation, a Bahraini organization headed by Khalid bin Hamad Al Khalifa, a son of King of Bahrain, Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa. A 2025 Amnesty International Report said Bahrain continued to "to suppress the rights to freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly, including through arbitrary detention and prosecutions."
Authoritarian links remain for MMA
Such links with authoritarian governments have become, Zidan added, fairly commonplace in the sport.

"They've already had associations with authoritarian regimes in the past and it's very likely that relationship will build. If this [the Asian Games and potential Olympic acceptance] means that we will now have more amateur MMA events being hosted around the world in youth championships, it's very likely that authoritarian regimes will jump on that."

The challenge for FIMMA, who appear to want to take MMA in the Olympic direction and away from UFC and its associations, is to make the sport more "normal" and less about spectacle, FIMMA's vice president Alex Engelhardt told AP.
"It's very challenging in the sense that the whole mindset in the sport is so focused on promotions," he said.
Even if that can change, and sport's debut at the Asian Games adds some legitimacy, the Olympics still seem some way off.

articles.title: EU spends three times more on imports from China than bloc exports there
articles.summary: Study shows trade deficit ran at more than €1bn a day in July, days before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump

blocks.text: Consumers and businesses in the EU are spending three times more on Chinese imports than their counterparts in China are buying from the bloc, a study has shown.
Customs data showed the gap between the EU’s imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1bn (£860m) a day in July.

The new data comes just days after the EU commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the trade imbalance must be arrested, and before Xi Jinping’s summit with Donald Trump on Thursday in Washington.
The Mercator Institute for China Studies (Meric) said: “The problem is no longer simply that the EU is buying more Chinese goods. China is selling more to Europe while buying less from it.”
China and the EU are locked in talks about averting a trade war, and the EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will travel to Beijing to meet his Chinese counterpart on 8 October.
“With the bilateral deficit now exceeding €1bn a day, the widening imbalance will almost certainly be high on the agenda at the planned EU-China meeting in October,” Meric said.

Analysis of Chinese customs data by Meric showed the EU’s trade deficit hit €36.5bn in July alone, up from €32.2bn in July 2025. From January to July the total deficit now stands at €234bn, about €21bn more than the first seven months of 2025.
“The imbalance has now moved beyond three to one. For every €1 of goods the EU exported to China in July, it imported €3.10. The deficit was equivalent to €1.18bn a day,” Meric said.
Sources in Brussels said one of the measures being considered is introducing quotas on hybrid vehicles and certain types of chemicals imported from China.

The Financial Times reported last week that the EU has asked China to voluntarily reduce exports of hybrids, as sales rocketed after the imposition of extra tariffs beyond the 10% levy applying to all third-country car imports.
The latest figures show imports of hybrid cars that do not have to be plugged in have grown tenfold from just under 4,000 vehicles sold in October 2024, to 50,000 in July 2026.
China has repeatedly warned it is ready for a trade war but its commerce ministry last week maintained diplomacy before the October summit.

“Any solution ​between China and the EU must ensure a ​balance of interests, comply ‌with World Trade Organization ​rules and ​the respective domestic laws of every side, and fully take into account the interests of industries on both sides,” it said.
Chinese exports will be high on the agenda at Thursday’s summit in Washington, with expectations that a 12-month suspension of Beijing’s rare earth export restrictions will be extended.

Kurt Tong, the former US consul general to Hong Kong and managing director of the Asia Group strategic advisory firm, said if a reprieve was not announced this week it could be announced at Asia Pacific Economic Corporation summit next month.
China introduced the rare earth export restrictions in April 2025, almost bringing the car industry in the EU, Mexico, US and the UK to a halt amid shortages of permanent magnets.
It suspended the ban last October when Trump met Xi in South Korea but did not offer any further concessions when the two presidents last met in May in Beijing.

articles.title: After Rappler report, more Gencorp contracts with Davao City Hall confirmed
articles.summary: PhilGEPS and Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte separately confirm that Gencorp's contracts with Davao City Hall are worth more than twice the amount previously reported

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) official, and even Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, confirmed that the company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte won more contracts than initially and exclusively reported by Rappler.

PhilGEPS division chief Rendell Sopeña told the impeachment court on Tuesday, September 22, that according to its database, Gencorp Industries bagged P34.2 million in projects with the Davao City government, more than twice the P14.3 million in contracts previously identified by Rappler in its September 15 report.

The younger Duterte said in a press release earlier Tuesday that Gencorp has P33.2 million in contracts with Davao City Hall since 2022, coinciding with the time his older sister became vice president and he assumed the mayorship of their hometown.

The Davao City mayor’s confirmatory statement came with a claim that he did not have knowledge of his sister’s ties to Gencorp, and an assertion that all of city hall’s deals with Gencorp were aboveboard.
“Any claim otherwise shall be duly supported with verified evidence and reliable documents,” Mayor Duterte said.
The Vice President’s name is not in any Securities and Exchange Commission filing of Gencorp, but she claimed to be its stockholder in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth.
The prosecution believes the findings strengthen its case of unexplained wealth against the Vice President, which it said is a betrayal of public trust and a culpable violation of the Constitution.

blocks.caption: After Rappler report, more Gencorp contracts with Davao City Hall confirmed

blocks.text: “This is where the conflict of interest comes in. Given the blood relationship between the local chief executive, Mayor Baste, and one of Gencorp’s shareholders, the company won a contract with city hall. On that aspect, there was a violation,” prosecution spokesman Zia Adiong said. “The Vice President should have divested.”
The 1987 Constitution explicitly prohibits the Vice President from maintaining business interests while in office.

articles.title: What is the White House press pool and why is it in a row with Trump?
articles.summary: The White House press pool is at the centre of a major row between President Donald Trump and TV networks. What is it?

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
A network boycott affected live TV coverage of Trump's ribbon-cutting event at the White House
When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event.
This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news – the White House Press pool.
Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications.
Coverage of upcoming presidential engagements, which include the UN General Assembly in New York, could be affected.
What is the White House press pool?
It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday.
There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category.

Material from the TV pool feed is shared between its members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - to save on costs and space. The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation.

The latest row began on Friday, when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team.
A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled.
On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events.

That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad. But with no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The TV network rotate coverage of White House events

blocks.text: The TV network rotate coverage of White House events
Why did US networks pull out of filming Trump?

Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump.
In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government.
"No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting."
The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms.

It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday.
In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting.
"Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."
Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday will be unaffected by the boycott because it will be carried by outlets which are not part of the pool.
But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout.
How has Trump reacted and what is Trump TV?
Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements.

"Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube.
Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place."
So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies.
For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York.
Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience.
In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.
There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access.
The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009.

But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.

articles.title: Iran war spreads through region as Trump seeks way out
articles.summary: Washington, Tehran and the Gulf states continue to pursue different objectives while searching for a way to end the Iran war.

image.caption: In addition to the Strait of Hormuz, the fighting is now affecting Saudi oil exports through the Red SeaImage: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nearly seven months into the Iran war, negotiations between Washington and Tehran have led nowhere, and the conflict has spread from the Strait of Hormuz to another strategically important shipping route.

In September, Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen took over critical positions on the Yemeni coast and are threatening Red Sea trade routes while launching attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia. This compounds a global energy crunch brought on by the Strait of Hormuz blockade.
Earlier in September, Saudi officials blamed Iran-backed militias in Iraq for blowing up the critical East-West oil pipeline.
According to The New York Times, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called US President Donald Trump on Sunday to once again urge him to intervene and stop the Houthi's rapid advance.

Trump is reported to have considered airstrikes against the Houthis at one point, but later abandoned the plans. This weekend, Fox News reported that Trump said the Houthi rebels had agreed not to attack US targets. The US news outlet Axios also reported that Trump had rejected a Saudi request for strikes against the Houthis the previous week.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?

Against the backdrop of record high gasoline and diesel prices coming down hard on voters ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections, US President Donald Trump is under pressure to show results in the Iran war.

"President Trump wants to end the Iran war from a position that allows him to claim that Iran's nuclear and military capabilities have been significantly weakened, freedom of navigation has been restored, and Tehran has been forced back to the negotiating table," Iran expert Fatemeh Aman told DW.

Aman, who has worked with organizations including the Middle East Institute, the Atlantic Council, RFE/RL and Voice of America, however, added that a coherent strategy for achieving these objectives remains difficult to discern.

The US has imposed high military and economic costs on Iran and appears to have made progress in weakening the country's military capabilities. But Tehran has not capitulated and there is no lasting ceasefire agreement.

Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this week. China is by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil and an important political partner of Tehran. The US president is likely to bring up China's economic and financial ties with Iran and hope that Beijing will use its influence over Tehran — particularly when it comes to the security of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

At the same time, Trump has signaled that he is open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is traveling to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Senior representatives from the Gulf states are also expected in the US over the coming days.
According to Axios, Trump plans to discuss the Iran war with representatives of several Gulf states on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route
Gulf nations want regional stability

There is still no common position emerging between Iran and its Arab neighbors in the Gulf. A planned meeting involving Iran, the Gulf states and Iraq was canceled last week. The cancellation may be linked to the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

"At first glance, there appears to be little common ground between Iran and the Gulf states," Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told DW. "But behind the scenes, there is at least a shared interest in preventing further military escalation."
The Gulf states recognize that they would be unlikely to prevail in a direct military confrontation with Iran, and generally favor de-escalation and a pragmatic easing of tensions with Tehran.
An agreement, however, is not currently in sight. In particular, Iran's demands for greater control over the Strait of Hormuz go too far from the perspective of the Gulf states.
The war in Yemen further limits the scope for rapprochement. Saudi Arabia, for example, is unlikely to make concessions while it remains under pressure from the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
Iran's two-track strategy
A permanently hostile, US-backed coalition of Gulf states would be strategically costly for Tehran, Aman said.

She added Iran could pursue a two-track strategy: This would involve resisting a US-led regional containment architecture, while simultaneously offering the Gulf states an alternative model of regional security based on accommodation and dialogue.
"After all, the Gulf states are not only Iran's rivals but also its neighbors — and neither side can change that geographic reality," Aman said.
According to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei, Tehran is demanding that the US end the fighting on all fronts.

Tehran is also calling for the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets and the lifting of the naval blockade in the strait. Talks with Qatar and Oman are reportedly continuing. The Iranian regime is now waiting for a response from Trump. Whether these diplomatic signals can translate into a broader political process remains uncertain.
For now, the main obstacle is that Washington, Tehran and the Gulf states continue to pursue very different roadmaps for ending the months-long conflict.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Doctor in court to face Rwanda genocide charges in UK
articles.summary: Dr Vincent Brown was charged following a seven year British investigation into the 1994 killings.

blocks.text: A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court.
He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings.
He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity.
The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday.
The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus.
The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994.
Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part."

Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack."
Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son.
The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime.
Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son.
In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda.
He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government.
Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation.
Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations."
He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day."
"These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."
Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

articles.title: Father admits causing death of his son in Cyprus hotel fall
articles.summary: The two-year-old boy fell from the window of a hotel in Cyprus in July, a Paphos court hears.

blocks.text: The man was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week in order for the plea hearing to take place.
His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing.
Paphos district court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side.
The father decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said.
A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing.
"The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said.
The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence.

articles.title: Turkey: Several pupils injured in shooting outside school
articles.summary: The shooter, a pupil, allegedly took a rifle and shot indiscriminately at his schoolmates in front of their high school. Turkey was shocked by two back-to-back school shootings earlier this year.

image.caption: Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the schoolImage: DHA

blocks.text: A shooting near a high school in Turkey's Manisa province resulted in at least 11 injured pupils, two of whom were in critical condition on Tuesday, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said.
The shooter, a pupil at the school, was arrested together with both of his parents and his grandfather.
What do we know about the shooting incident?
The suspect is said to have taken the weapon from his grandparents' house, with his grandfather believed to have had a licence for it.
Local authorities said the attack took place at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district at about 08:00am local time (07:00 CET).
The motive for the shooting is also under investigation. Some reports suggest the student had suffered from bullying.

blocks.caption: Two back-to-back school shootings in April left around 10 killed and dozens more injuredImage: Ensar Ozdemir/REUTERS

blocks.text: "When the ​security of our children is the issue, it is not possible for any ​negligence, any irresponsibility to be overlooked," the minister posted on his X account.

"The ‌circumstances under which the child obtained the gun used in the attack, the conditions of the weapon's storage, the parents' obligations regarding care ‌and supervision, and allegations of bullying prior to the incident ‌are ​being investigated thoroughly and from multiple angles," Gurlek added.
Footage posted online showed a male carrying a rifle near the school, while police told families to stay away from the area.
Gun control tightened after school shootings
School shootings are rare in Turkey, but this year alone saw two back-to-back shootings that shocked the nation.
Two school shootings that took place in April resulted in the tightening of gun controls and the increase of security measures at educational facilities as the academic year started last week.
Several students and their teacher were killed in one of the attacks, with the other resulting in 16 people being injured.
According to Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci, 31,000 school supervisors and police officers on duty were assigned to school seen as being at risk, as per a new measure introduced only on Monday.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan responded to the latest shooting attack by promising even tighter gun controls.
"When we look at similar attacks around the world, especially in the United States, we see one of the perpetrators' aims is to terrorise society," the Turkish leader said.

articles.title: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses
articles.summary: 'Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensya,' prosecutor Terry Ridon quips

blocks.text: Graphics by Nico Villarete/Rappler
'Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensya,' prosecutor Terry Ridon quips
Even the country’s top fast food chain was not spared in the expansive investigation into Vice President Sara Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.
Could Jollibee hold a piece of the smoking gun that the prosecution has been searching for to remove her from office?

Jollibee was implicated in the mess because documents show that its Bolton Street branch in Davao City is owned by Gencorp Industries Inc., described in one of government documents as a franchisee of the casual dining giant.

Duterte said in her sworn Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) that she is a stockholder of Gencorp, although her name is not in Securities and Exchange Commission documents (SEC) filings of the company.

Other companies associated with the Vice President or her husband Mans Carpio are Metro City Chow Food Corporation, City Hall King Chow Foods Corporation, Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., and Great Jolly Times Food Corp.
The names of several of these companies appear to echo those of Jollibee and its sister fast-food chain, Chowking.

“This P2.1 billion in sales — these are restaurants, right? Are they Jollibee or Chowking?” Senator Kiko Pangilinan asked. “I would assume there are many Jollibee and Chowking franchises, which is why sales reached billions over a period of time.”
“One of the financial statements that the witness identified yesterday contains the word ‘Jollibee’ in reference to Gencorp,” prosecutor Erwin Matib said. “Yes, there are franchises.”
Jollibee Davao Bolton is a known hangout spot of the Dutertes. It is in the same building as the listed address of Gencorp.

Rappler previously reported that Gencorp has cornered at least P14 million in contracts with Davao City Hall since 2022, coinciding with the time that Sara became VP, and her brother Sebastian assumed the mayorship of their hometown.

The Davao City mayor later not only confirmed the existence of the deals, but even updated the actual total value of the contracts bagged by Gencorp — P33 million over 19 contracts. Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System division chief Rendell Sopeña told the impeachment court that there are 15 Gencorp-Davao City deals worth P34 million in its database.

The arrangement raises questions on conflict of interest, and potential violation of the Constitution. The 1987 charter explicitly prohibits the Vice President from having business interests while in office.
The Jollibee connection did not escape the prosecution and her critics, which used its slogan to take a swipe at the Vice President.
“Bida ang sarap, bida ang ebidensiya (the star is the flavor, the star is the evidence),” prosecutor Terry Ridon said.

blocks.caption: Jollibee enters the menu as impeach court scrutinizes Sara Duterte businesses

blocks.text: “Inday, pa-Jollibee ka naman diyan (Inday, how about treating us to Jollibee),” former presidential adviser Ronald Llamas said in jest on Facebook.
Spectators of the trial might just be craving two things after Tuesday’s proceedings: a one-piece Chickenjoy, and an explanation from the Vice President. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘The choice was prison or exile’: journalists who fled Russia publish grim portrait of Putin
articles.summary:
Roman Badanin and Mikhail Rubin, who were forced to move abroad in 2021, tell of president capable of ‘limitless cruelty’

At 6am on 29 June 2021, the Russian journalist Roman Badanin was…

blocks.text: At 6am on 29 June 2021, the Russian journalist Roman Badanin was woken by a knock on the door of his family’s Moscow apartment. “Come quickly, someone has scratched your car in the courtyard,” a voice shouted from outside. As he opened the door, masked men pushed their way in.

Across the city, a similar raid was happening at the home of Badanin’s colleague Mikhail Rubin. The masked men were officers of the FSB, the Russian intelligence service, instruments of the “climate of fear and violence” that the journalists say Vladimir Putin has imposed on Russia in their forensically detailed biography of the Russian president.

The Tsar in Person is almost 800 pages and has won the Grand Prix Strasbourg, a French literary award, whose jury said it read like a “spy novel” and praised the “courage and commitment” of the authors during decades of investigating reporting.

For Badanin and Rubin, the dawn raids were a warning. As founders of the independent media project Proekt, specialising in investigative journalism, both men had been threatened, interrogated, labelled traitors and foreign agents, banned from news events and had offices searched. Other colleagues had not been so lucky: several had died suddenly or in unexplained accidents or seemingly random attacks.

Rubin told the Guardian: “The first time we were threatened was in 2019 when we published an investigation into the chief of Putin’s propaganda operation. A Kremlin official warned me the consequences might be scary. Security agents visited my parents and asked them why I, their son, was selling out his country, betraying Russia.”

After the FSB agents’ dawn raid, Rubin discovered his passport placed carefully on a table. “It was a message. If they’d taken it, I wouldn’t be allowed to leave the country, but they wanted me to leave so they put it where I would see it,” he said. “At the time I didn’t plan on leaving. I didn’t want to overthink the danger because I thought they were just trying to stop me working.”
Less than three weeks later, the Kremlin declared Proekt an “undesirable” media outlet. “I left Moscow the next morning,” Rubin said.
Badanin, who was on holiday with his family in Morocco, decided it was too dangerous for him to return. “The choice was prison or exile and I didn’t want to go to prison.”

blocks.caption: Roman Badanin (left) and Mikhail Rubin. Composite: Wikipedia and Proekt

blocks.text: Their book, so far published only in Russian and French, charts the rise of Putin from an unremarkable clerk and undercover KGB agent at St Petersburg city hall to the Kremlin, where he has clung to power since 2000.

It is not the first biography to portray the president and his circle of cronies as cruel and corrupt, but the devil is in the encyclopaedic detail. Badanin and Rubin, both former Kremlin-accredited “pool” journalists, have 40 years of investigative journalism between them and have conducted hundreds of interviews to produce a grim portrait of Putin.

They depict him as a modern-day tsar, without ideology or convictions, a dictator capable of “limitless cruelty” who sees himself as above morality and laws. Rivals and opponent, or simply those who have become inconvenient, meet unexpected ends in accidents, crashes and falls, or are poisoned with toxins and radioactive particles causing agonising deaths.

“These pages are the result of war and repression, of exile and the death of some of those close to us, the suffering of friends thrown in prison,” the pair write. “We hope it will contribute to destroying the circumstances that have made all this misfortune possible and defeat the person who did this with his own hands.”

It is also the story of Russia from the end of the Soviet Union to today. Badanin says the book is aimed at young Russians who have no idea what their country was like before Putin took power. Unsurprisingly, it is banned by the Kremlin.

Badanin told Le Monde: “We’re also targeting audiences abroad, where many myths about Putin are circulating. There’s no need to invent myths about Putin. Let the facts reveal the truth about him and his system.
“The Kremlin leader has no ideology. The war in Ukraine has made this clear: this war is not an extension of his ideas, it is merely a means of staying in power.”

Today, even thousands of miles from Moscow, neither journalist feels entirely safe from what they call “Putin’s death squads” dispatched to murder dissident Russians abroad to demonstrate the Kremlin’s long arms.
Last year, FBI agents turned up at Badanin’s California home to warn him they had information that he was at risk of an attack “by foreign special services”.
“I feel a little bit safer here than in Europe, but not completely safe,” Badanin said.

blocks.text: US TV networks suspend White House pool coverage over Trump media ban
Ariana Baio
The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds.
The collective decision came after the barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights.

The ban was an extraordinary escalation of Trump’s battle against news outlets. After a coalition of networks including ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – which along with CNN form a press “pool” that share the responsibilities of capturing and distributing footage of the president carried by news outlets worldwide – announced they would cease coverage in solidarity with the barred outlets, the White House promoted its own feed online, branding it “Trump TV”. The channel purported to show “top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place”.
“Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” the White House posted on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most – straight from the Trump Administration.”

It is extremely rare for a president to travel or make public appearances without the accompaniment of a representative from the White House television pool. Network cameras have provided coverage of the president since 1950.

On Monday, the ban against CNN meant that no broadcaster was covering Trump’s midday ribbon-cutting to unveil a new White House helipad. Although the White House provided a livestream, without professional boom mics and audio setup, the president’s remarks were inaudible over the sounds of a helicopter’s engine running in the background.

The president abruptly announced his ban against outlets this weekend in a Truth Social post, saying he had enough of “purposely negative stories” about him. Journalists had their press badges confiscated by Secret Service on Saturday.
Trump set for UN meetings with war on agenda as speech looms
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump is expected to ⁠start the day with a speech to assembled delegates at the UN General Assembly, before meeting with no fewer than 11 world leaders, bilaterally or in group settings.

While the contents of his speech are unknown, Trump last year caused a ⁠stir with a combative address, telling the audience that their countries were “going to hell” for, among other things, climate policy and mass migration.
The president is then set for a whirlwind schedule of meetings with ⁠leaders from four continents on Tuesday.
It comes against the backdrop of an unstable Middle East and a four-and-a-half-year-old war in Ukraine that shows no signs of abating.

Trump will meet with British prime minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian ‌president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Venezuela’s interim leader Delcy ‌Rodriguez, Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and the representatives of the Gulf states of the United Arab Emirates, ‌Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar.

In the evening, he may meet dozens more leaders, albeit briefly, during a leaders’ reception. Trump met with French president Emmanuel Macron on Monday and additions to his Tuesday schedule are possible.
Here, my colleague Robert Tait provides some analysis on what may be expected from Trump’s address:
In other developments:

items: The major US television news outlets agreed to suspend their video coverage of Donald Trump after the administration banned journalists from several outlets from entering the White House grounds. Newsrooms including the New York Times and the Washington Post also decided to hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage on Monday until midnight as part of the collective effort. More here.

The barred outlets – CNN, MS Now and Politico – sued the administration on Monday, saying the president’s actions were a violation of their first amendment rights. The parties are seeking a temporary restraining order that would immediately lift the ban – and return access for the journalists – while the case plays out. More here.

Trump is bracing for a loss in the lawsuit brought by the three media organizations, as he considers that the judge presiding over the case – his own appointee – previously ordered the White House to restore credentials for journalist Jim Acosta. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote on Truth Social.

Trump said that he hoped Zohran Mamdani would be a “great mayor” for New York, an unusually warm assessment of the democratic socialist leader whom the president and his Republican allies have spent months holding up as a symbol of the Democratic party’s alleged embrace of “communism” ahead of the November midterms. More here.

The Venezuelan man who was shot by a federal immigration officer in Texas on Sunday spoke out from detention on Monday afternoon when he was able to call his lawyer, in the middle of a press conference, and plead for better medical care. Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was taken from a hospital in Austin into Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention, even though he apparently still has a bullet lodged near his spine and is in much discomfort. More here.

Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Republican subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet, has said the allegations are untrue – and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her. More here.
