articles.title: Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's 2020 death case has been reopened
articles.summary: Disha Salian's father insists her death was not suicide or an accident, but that she was gang-raped and murdered.

blocks.text: On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel.
She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration.
As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days.
It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive.
On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead.
Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai.
Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally.
Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide.
But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death.

The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered.

His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years.

In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years.
The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers".

They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall.
"We find this difficult to accept," they wrote.

One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime.
Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him.
The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case.

Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput.

"She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added.
Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote.
In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home.
Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment.

But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues.

Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death.
In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked.

Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain.

"In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused."

In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them".

But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta.

items: Sushant Singh Rajput: Mystery and voyeurism around Bollywood star's death
Rhea Chakraborty: Why is Indian TV obsessed with Sushant Singh Rajput's death?
Sushant Singh Rajput: Rhea Chakraborty on 'media trial' after Bollywood star's death

blocks.text: Satish Salian, who's been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter, says he's felt "some peace" after the court ordered the fresh investigation into her death.
Disha, he told the BBC, was "very bright, she did well in her studies and read a lot. She had a heart of gold and was very helpful. She was our only child and she loved us very much".
His wife, he says, has been unable to come to terms with her tragic death and has gone into depression.
"I want the death penalty for those who hurt my daughter. Those who inflicted pain on her must die a painful death too. That is what justice for Disha would look like to me," he says.

articles.title: Canadian investigation launched into data breach that exposed millions of IDs
articles.summary: Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued…

image.caption: Canada's privacy commissioner is investigating a data security breach that exposed identification details from driver's licences and other government-issued ID. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Canada's privacy commissioner has launched an investigation into a data breach at IDScan.net that potentially exposed details from millions of driver's licences and other kinds of government-issued identification from Canada and the U.S.
Privacy commissioner will look into IDScan.net breach involving Canada-issued driver's licences
IDScan.net provides identification verification software to several categories of businesses, from bars and casinos to car rental companies.

Earlier this month, the company published a public notice about a data security incident, stating that "an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud."

items: Woman flagged by ID scanner as nationwide 'public safety concern' after incident in Winnipeg bar
ID scan technology at Alcanna liquor stores collected too much data, says investigation

blocks.text: The company said it was notifying individuals who had potentially been affected and offered free credit monitoring services.

Two days before IDScan.net published its alert, the FBI confirmed it was looking into the reported theft of tens of millions of driver's licences belonging to people in the U.S. and Canada that were being sold on the dark net.
The bureau said it was “looking into the incident” but could not comment “due to the ongoing nature of the investigation.”
Unprecedented in size and scope
The breach could be one of the largest-ever exposures of government-issued identity documents in North America.
Zach Edwards, a threat researcher at the cybersecurity company Infoblox, told Reuters the incident was unprecedented in terms of its sweep.

"There's never been a breach of driver's licences at this scale," said Edwards, who added that he discovered his own license was part of it. Edwards said that the ongoing nature of the breach "means that this attack created legitimate national security risks for high-profile individuals."

Canada's Office of the Privacy Commissioner says it's examining the security safeguards IDScan.net had in place at the time of the breach and whether its actions to notify potentially affected Canadians were adequate.
The probe will also look at whether IDScan.net breached Canada’s federal private-sector privacy laws.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: This American town runs an annual festival celebrating Canada. It hit different this year
articles.summary: Channon Mondoux grew up in Windsor, Ont., married an American and eventually made a home with her family in Kalamazoo, Mich. On Saturday, Mondoux helped host the fourth annual Can-Am Peace Jam, a…

image.caption: Festival-goers smile at this year's Can-Am Peace Jam in Kalamazoo, Mich. (Dare'l McMillian)

blocks.text: As It Happens·Q&A

Channon Mondoux grew up in Windsor, Ont., married an American and eventually made a home with her family in Kalamazoo, Mich. On Saturday, Mondoux helped host the fourth annual Can-Am Peace Jam, a festival celebrating Canadian culture and the longstanding ties between the two countries.
Founder, a Canadian living in Michigan, says current tensions just make her more determined
LISTEN | Full interview with Channon Russette-Mondoux:
As It Happens6:06This American town runs an annual festival celebrating Canada. It hit different this year
Channon Russette-Mondoux, grew up in Windsor, Ont., married an American and eventually made a home with her family in Kalamazoo, Mich.
But she never lost her connection to Canada — and she’s now turned that tie into an annual celebration.
On Saturday, Russette-Mondoux helped host the fourth annual Can-Am Peace Jam, a festival celebrating Canadian culture and the longstanding ties between the two countries.

That sense of cross-border friendship comes at a time when relations between Canada and the U.S. have been anything but smooth, amid an ongoing trade war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s talk of making Canada the 51st U.S. state.
In Kalamazoo, though, the focus holds onto the hope that Canadians and Americans can still come together.

This year's event featured Canadian and local bands playing hits by artists including Rush, Bryan Adams, Alanis Morissette, Avril Lavigne and Nickelback. There was also a curling demonstration, arts and crafts from local vendors, and a genealogist helping festivalgoers trace their Canadian roots.
Russette-Mondoux spoke with As It Happens host Nil Köksal about why she started the festival, what the Can-Am Peace Jam means to her community and why she believes it’s important to keep it going.
I know this is a labour of love for you but I wonder after all these years whether this year, this weekend, felt different.
Sometimes it's hard. It is hard because I love my homeland so much, which is the impetus for this really, and I think when it gets harder out there, it drives me harder to keep going.
You designed this as a celebration, but I wonder in this moment how people are reacting?

Americans, for the most part, are completely devastated over what is happening with Canada. The average person on the street is mortified to hear the things that are being said, to see the policies that are being enacted.

The festival is absolutely not about politics; it's about people. But I am also involved in my community, and I became a U.S. citizen for the sole purpose of being able to vote, and I am committed, just like I was in Canada. I was committed to my country [and] I'm committed to community here.
The name has changed from the Canadiana festival to the Can-Am Peace Jam. You were calling yourself a peace officer. When did you decide to make that change?

We started out as Canadianafest for the first two years, and then in 2025, when there was a lot of rhetoric starting to come out, and I knew the minute I had heard the words — 51st state coming as a joke or [Mark Carney as] the governor of Canada and all that coming out — I knew right away that we were headed for a mess of trouble.

I made a point of it [among] all this chirping going on out there [to say] ‘Let's put that away because what we do is joyful’ regardless of what anyone else says. We're gonna come together, regardless of what anybody else says.’

We called it the Can-Am Peace Jam but what we realized is that the Canadiana Fest became the organization — the celebration of Canadian culture became the organization — and the festival became the Can-Am Peace Jam, because we do things all year round.
We're doing hockey watch parties, poutine parties, Boxing Day parties. We even supported the very first street hockey program in inner-city Kalamazoo.
The vice mayor of Kalamazoo takes part [and] was a judge at the best butter tart contest at the festival. That's one of the things that happened on the weekend. What are some of the other events?

Traditionally, we have a poutine competition called the World Champion Poutine Competition, and we've had six, seven, eight food trucks competing with various kinds of poutine. This year, unfortunately, they had to step back because we had to move the festival indoors after the realization that the storm front that was coming through on Saturday would have just shut us down.

We pivoted and reached out to a community businessman named Harvin Sandhu Singh, who happens to have ties to Canada, and he agreed to let us come into his 30,000 square foot facility in downtown Kalamazoo and use it for our festival, and so we were lucky enough to pull it off.
Do you ever have people who aren't fans of what you're doing and push back at the idea?

You're always going to hear somebody chirping about something, right? I mean, the internet is the internet. I think everybody looks for an opportunity to say something negative about something else. We're not Pollyannas, we know that there are people out there who have drank the Kool-Aid, that totally believe everything that comes out of the administration, and so they have a bee in their bonnet.
They're looking for something to be angry at. Considering the level of messaging that comes out of the White House, I'm shocked it hasn't been more.

I could tell just even from our conversation that this is emotional for you. Like a lot of people, as you said, you have two places that you call home. Does a time like this make you miss Canada more?

Yeah. It's hard sometimes and sometimes you just wanna hear the lilt of a Canadian voice, sometimes you just want to hear that more gentle approach, sometimes you wanna be standing in line and having a conversation, and you can fall into things that you grew up with, things that you're familiar with, and also just the attitude about not being so harsh, and that's what I think is a big difference between Canada and the U.S., is that Canadians are more laid back, but they're also a very fierce people. We're tenacious. We don't give up.
Oh God, I hope this will be over soon.

When this is over, and we will look back, and there've been other times, we've been through similar situations [like] during the depression, there were heavy tariffs put on Canada, [which] actually backfired like it's doing this time.
We have been through tough times in the past, and we can get back to being friends again, but I don't want to let a year go by without celebrating my homeland, and I'm not gonna hide, not gonna run.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Catherine Zhu is a writer and associate producer for CBC Radio. Her reporting interests include arts and culture, science and social justice. She holds a master's degree in journalism from the University of British Columbia. You can reach her at catherine.zhu@cbc.ca.
Audio produced by Emma Marshall. Q&A edited for length and clarity.

articles.title: Healthcare in Africa ‘under growing strain’ after US withdrawal from aid programs, report warns
articles.summary: Accra Reset’s report states countries in the region and global south should take greater control of their health development after USAID debacle The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.

The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.

The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.
A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.

The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.
External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.

The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.
Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.

At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.

The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.

“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”
Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.

“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”

The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.

The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.
The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

articles.title: U.S. shouldn't buy 'blood potash' from Belarus, Sask. premier says
articles.summary: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump posted on Monday that he is working on a potash deal with Belarus. (Alexander Quon/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe defended the province's potash industry as ethically and economically superior to other international exporters after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to source more of his country's fertilizer from Belarus.
Moe defends Sask. potash in post aimed at Trump's latest trade threat
"Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression," Moe said in a post on social media. "It’s wrong and it doesn’t make sense."
Moe's post on Monday afternoon was a response to a Trump social media post from earlier that day.

"The United States is working on ​a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash ​from Belarus," Trump said on Truth Social. "The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for ​our Farmers and Ranchers."

items: Trump says U.S. working on deal to buy potash from Belarus instead of Canada

blocks.text: Potash is mainly used in fertilizers. In 2024, almost a third of the world's potash production came from Canada and all of the country's 10 active potash mines are in Saskatchewan, according to Natural Resources Canada.
"More than 40 countries — Canada and its allies — have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine," Moe said in his social media post.

"Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan — right here in North America?"

Nutrien Ltd., The Mosaic Company, Compass Minerals, and K+S Potash Canada are responsible for all of Canada's potash production. BHP is building the Jansen potash mine in Saskatchewan and expects to start commercial production in mid-2027.

items: Sask. is a potash and agriculture giant. So why is conflict in the Middle East a problem for farmers?

blocks.text: Nutrien is the largest potash fertilizer producer in Canada and one of the largest in the world. The Saskatoon-based company referred CBC to Fertilizer Canada when asked to comment on Trump's post.
U.S. farmers have used Canadian potash for decades, said Fertilizer Canada, an industry trade group, in an emailed statement to CBC News.
"Reliability, proximity, transportation infrastructure, product availability and the ability to deliver during critical application windows all matter," the statement said.
"A strong and integrated North American fertilizer supply chain helps support farm productivity, affordability and food security on both sides of the border.”
Last year, Nutrien announced plans to build a potash export terminal at the Port of Longview, Wash., to handle expected growth in international demand for its fertilizer products.
The opposition NDP called Trump's social media post "infuriating" in a statement on Monday.
"He is looking at signing a deal with an authoritarian Russian satellite state that is supporting Putin’s brutal war against the people of Ukraine," the NDP statement said.
"This is a bad idea that will only hurt families and communities on both sides of the border."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jeremy Warren is a reporter in Saskatoon. You can reach him at jeremy.warren@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UK: Man charged over suspected role in Rwanda genocide
articles.summary: The suspect has been accused of directing and inciting acts of murder and genocide carried out by others in Rwanda.

image.caption: Over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus ⁠were killed in the 1994 genocide [FILE: April 4, 2014]Image: SIMON MAINA/AFP

blocks.text: UK authorities arrested and charged a man on Monday over alleged links to the Rwandan genocide, prosecutors and the London police said. It was the first arrest of its kind, although authorities have been pursuing the case for several years.
The 65-year-old man has been charged with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offenses of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, officials said.
"This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes," said Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing.

The Rwandan genocide took place in 1994, where over 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and moderate ethnic Hutus ⁠were killed in a 100-day rampage, orchestrated and led by the Hutu ruling majority. Local officials and ordinary citizens were involved in the mass killing.
UK law allows prosecutors to bring charges for some international offenses, including genocide and crimes against humanity, even if the crimes were committed abroad.

It is the latest case of an arrest in Europe of someone linked to Rwanda's genocide. In July, a German-Rwandan national was arrested for charges of taking part in the genocide and killing one person himself.
Meanwhile, in the Netherlands, a man was sentenced to life in prison for having taken part in attacks on homes, including launching a grenade on sheltering Tutsi civilians.
Survivors remember Rwanda's 1994 genocide
Suspect underwent name change
UK's Metropolitan Police war crimes investigators opened the case against the suspect in 2019, following a request by the Rwandan government.
The 65-year-old is originally from Kigali but lived in London at the time of the arrest.
He reportedly entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998, according to Rwandan Justice Minister Tharcisse Karugarama.
After being granted British citizenship in 2004, the man underwent a name change, and two years later, he was arrested over his connection to the genocide.
His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was ultimately halted by a British UK court in 2017.
The failed extradition prompted the Rwandan government to urge UK authorities to investigate the matter themselves.
Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's counterterror division, said the man is "alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others."
Authorities say investigations are ongoing for more suspects who are linked to the Rwandan genocide currently living in Britain.

articles.title: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
articles.summary: Andy Burnham says he will urge Donald Trump to bring an end to conflict with Iran The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore…

blocks.text: The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump.

The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil.

Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world.

The ongoing turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government.

On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.

“We have received a request from Saudi Arabia for military support and … I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling. On cost of living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain, the wider region … we need to keep those pathways open,” Burnham said.

The prime minister also plans to press Trump to wind down US action in Iran, which has destabilised the region, blocked key supply chains and unleashed global economic volatility, including in the UK where the government will struggle to drive down the cost of living as a result.

“Of course the message is that we want to see an end to the conflict as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part,” Burnham said when asked if he would raise the issue in talks with Trump.

As well as the focus on the Middle East, other major international challenges, including the war in Ukraine and artificial intelligence, are expected to dominate Burnham’s meetings at the United Nations general assembly.

The global security backdrop to the summit is bleak, with European leaders warning that Russia could launch a drone or missile attack on Nato territory within months to test the strength of the alliance.

Burnham’s speech to the UN is expected to focus on harnessing the power of AI, amid concerns at home over the safety of the rapidly advancing technology, and he will be accompanied on the trip by his AI minister, Kanishka Narayan.

Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump is a significant moment, with the US president still said to be angry over the UK’s refusal to support his military action in Iran, and ongoing tensions over levels of defence spending.

Government insiders, however, are taking some solace from Trump’s low-key response to UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, after weeks of diplomacy with the White House over the summer.

They are also hoping to avoid a clash over energy policy, with the prime minister expected to signal to Trump that he is in favour of more drilling in the North Sea, with the Jackdaw gas field likely to get the green light within weeks.

Analysts believe the balance of risk for the bilateral relationship has shifted since Keir Starmer was in office, with the Republicans facing a difficult set of midterm elections and the US president’s personal ratings plummeting.
Trump is also likely to be more focused on his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and his address to the UN general assembly, which comes shortly before the talks on Tuesday.

Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would try to pursue a “third way” in his relationship with the US president, neither as adversarial as the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, nor as publicly fawning as Starmer’s early approach, and relying on the strength of his personality.

articles.title: As Trump-Xi summit nears, Europe is caught in middle of US-China rivalry
articles.summary: China's Xi Jinping is traveling to Washington this week. Regardless of what comes from his talks with US President Trump, the EU will likely remain stuck between erratic US trade policy and Beijing's…

image.caption: Donald Trump is set to meet Xi Jinping for the third time this week since returning to office in January 2025Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: German and Chinese business leaders met in the German city of Düsseldorf for an economic dialogue last week. Although the panel focused on trade and investment between China and Europe, ongoing US-China rivalry was the elephant in the room.

As Xi Jinping and Donald Trump sit down in the US capital Washington this week, there is some hope that talks will show progress on alleviating the ongoing trade war launched by the US president. The last time the two leaders met at a Beijing summit in May did not yield any tangible results.

"The assumption in Beijing, and that's the way they're operating, is that China and the US will hold each other in check for the foreseeable future," Mikko Huotari, director of the Berlin-based China think tank MERICS, told a policy briefing last week.

"Xi really doesn't need a breakthrough in Washington. He needs more time. And the same is true for Washington. So we have this strategic stalemate situation, which I think is the best description of what we see currently."
A deal could benefit Trump's Republican Party ahead of the important US midterm elections in November, but that outcome remains far from certain.
"We will discuss everything," Trump said about Xi's visit to the White House.
Cooperation on AI?
Beijing and Washington are competing on multiple levels and nowhere is this rivalry more consequential than with artificial intelligence (AI).
The US government prohibits the export of high-performance chips to China. Beijing, in turn, restricts the export of rare earth elements, which are indispensable for semiconductor production.

And amid concerns about the dangers of unregulated AI, there is some expectation that Xi and Trump will discuss AI guardrails during their talks. Xi has called for international cooperation on AI development, while Trump sees its regulation as a threat to the US' leadership in the field.

After meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that US and Chinese officials have already discussed creating a "notification mechanism" to share information about AI-related security incidents.
AI's expanding power alarms China's intelligence agency
Europe's 'China shock'
From a European perspective, both China and the US are currently considered difficult partners.
The second "China shock … is already here" in Europe, said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in her 2026 State of the Union address last week.
The first "China shock" came 25 years ago, triggered by China's accession to the World Trade Organization (WTO), when inexpensive "Made in China" products began to flood the global markets.
The second one stems from China's technological progress in industries such as battery technology, green energy and mobility.
"It shows in our communities and in factories across our Union. It leads to deindustrialization in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable," von der Leyen said in her address.

The EU is aiming for a rapid transition to e-mobility and wants to drastically reduce CO2 emissions from road traffic. At the same time, Brussels is calling for additional tariffs on low-cost electric cars from China, as China enjoys competitive advantages with cheaper cars and high government subsidies.
China denies having an unfair advantage, and German automakers VW and BMW also oppose punitive tariffs due to potential revenue losses resulting from Chinese retaliatory measures.
What new alliances will reshape the world?
A Chinese participant at the Düsseldorf economic dialogue told DW anonymously that China's domestic consumption cannot absorb manufacturing.

"China's economy is weak. Companies are worried about their business and urgently need to tap into foreign markets," said the Chinese executive, who used to work in the European branch of a Chinese state-owned enterprise.
Trump pressuring EU over China, but also on trade, security

"Against the backdrop of the ongoing escalation of strategic rivalry between the US and China, the US is constantly urging its allies to tighten restrictions on China in the areas of technology, supply chains, and security," said Yang Xiepu, director of the Center for Sino-German Cooperation at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).
Trade Reset: How Europe is replacing China and the US

At the same time, Trump frequently threatens the EU with tariffs while injecting instability into the strategic NATO alliance. When the EU offered Canada "associate membership" last week, Trump floated the possibility of new punitive measures from the US.
While Carney expressed interest, Trump called the idea "ridiculous."

"If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump said, without specifying what he considers about EU-Canada ties to be "hostile."
Copying Canada's 'middle' approach
Facing the Trump administration's tariff upsets and caustic rhetoric, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is openly hedging his bets on the world stage.

"We know the old order is not coming back. We shouldn't mourn it," he declared at the 2026 World Economic Forum in Davos in January, with the US allies rattled by Trump threatening to annex Greenland from Denmark.
Carney said that great powers can "afford for now to go it alone," but middle powers need to work better together.

"When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what's offered. We compete with each other to be the most accommodating. This is not sovereignty," Carney told the forum.
"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he emphasized.

In early 2026, Carney visited China and agreed to a "new-era strategic partnership." Ottawa subsequently lowered import tariffs on Chinese electric cars from 100% to 6.1%. The quota stands at 49,000 vehicles per year.
Separately, China has launched a charm offensive toward US allies, "more specifically, the fragile allies," according to MERICS Director Mikko Huotari.

For example, Xi attended the BRICS summit in India in September despite the rocky relationship with New Delhi. He also attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan before that. After meeting with Trump this week in Washington, he is expected to travel to the US again in December for the G20 summit in Miami, though that might depend on Donald Trump attending the APECsummit hosted by China in November.

Canada's Carney has described this new form of diplomacy as "variable geometry" — different alliances for different issues based on common values and interests. In November, Carney is se to travel to Shenzhen for the APEC summit. He will also be at the table there — and hopefully not on the menu.
A new Cold War: Can the middle powers forge a path forward?
Correction: A previous version of this article stated that China will be hosting a G20 summit in November, rather than an APEC summit. This has now been corrected. We apologize for the error.

Students faced prison terms and thousands of dollars in restitution over campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza

Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and…

blocks.text: Five Stanford University students who faced prison sentences and thousands of dollars in restitution in connection to a campus protest against Israel’s war on Gaza had all charges dropped on Monday.
The students also had their restitution severely reduced, ending a two-year legal saga that also saw the lead prosecutor in the case removed by the court.

Part of a group of 12, the students had been charged with felony conspiracy to trespass and felony vandalism in connection to an hour-long, June 2024 occupation during which the group barricaded themselves inside the university president’s office to demand Stanford consider a student resolution to divest from Israel, among other requests.

Some accepted plea deals or other diversion offers but five of the students went to trial earlier this year. The month-long trial ended with a hung jury but Jeff Rosen, the Santa Clara county district attorney, immediately announced his intention to retry the case before a judge ordered his recusal in May over a conflict of interest that, the judge said during court proceedings, would “render it unlikely that the defendants will receive fair treatment”.

The case has since been taken over by the California attorney general’s office, which reached a resolution with the students. That resolution meant dropping all charges in exchange for 100 hours of community service at a nonprofit of their choosing and a total restitution of about $50,000, far less than the $1m prosecutors initially threatened them with and the $ 329,000 they each risked being found liable for at trial. The charges were the most severe handed out against students in connection to pro-Palestine protests on campus.
A spokesperson for Rosen referred questions about the case to the California attorney general’s office.
The attorney general’s office and Stanford University did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment.
Three of the students who had previously accepted misdemeanor pleas will also have their convictions withdrawn as part of Monday’s agreement once they complete the required community service.

Two of the defendants who went to trial earlier this year, German Gonzalez and Amy Zhai, spoke of their relief in exclusive interviews with the Guardian. The ordeal severely upended their lives and they shared their deep frustration at what they saw as Stanford and Rosen’s effort to criminalize and silence speech in support of Palestinians. They said that they hoped their win would encourage other students to continue to speak out.

“The most significant part of this is that I can continue to be involved in the Palestine movement in ways that were kind of curtailed by also being actively a defendant in a criminal case,” said Zhai, who graduated from Stanford as the trial got under way and is now in law school at a different university. “[The prosecution] was intended to silence speech about Palestine, and for everything that they threw at this case, they have failed.”

Zhai added: “People still very much care about Palestine but I think they are afraid, and reasonably so, because of everything that’s happened with the escalation of repression over the past two years. It takes victories like this one to encourage people to turn their beliefs into action.”

Thousands of students were arrested over their involvement in pro-Palestinian campus protests in the spring of 2024. Dozens were suspended or expelled from their universities, but most of those who also faced criminal charges have seen those charges dropped.

Abbee Cox, a member of the Stanford students’ legal team, told the Guardian that Monday’s resolution was in line with those reached in other cases relating to campus protests, which have mostly ended in diversion deals rather than severe sentences.

“The attorney general’s office has addressed this in a manner consistent with the way other peaceful student protesters at Stanford have been treated over the years – protesters against apartheid, against the Vietnam War,” she said. “But it took almost two and a half years of this painful and protracted and incredibly stressful battle to get there. And it took a fair prosecutor to get us there in the end.”

As protests flared up on campuses across the country in the first year of the Gaza war, the Stanford students briefly occupied the president’s office, renaming the building after Adnan al-Bursh, a Palestinian surgeon who was reportedly tortured to death while in Israeli detention.

They were immediately arrested, suspended, and banned from campus for two terms, but it was not until a year later, in April 2025, that Rosen announced criminal charges against the group, declaring at a press conference that “dissent is American, vandalism is criminal”.

Rosen was ultimately removed from the case in May, after the students’ legal team submitted evidence to the court that he had used the pending case to fundraise for his re-election, citing it in a webpage dedicated to showcasing his work to fight against “antisemitism”. The page was also emailed to a listserv of more than 600 people, soliciting donations. Rosen responded to the recusal effort by accusing the student’s defense attorney of engaging in a “f—— antisemitic trope” in an interview with a local publication.

In pre-trial motions, Rosen had sought to ban the students from discussing “genocide”, as well as the political motivations behind the protest and free speech issues – a request the court denied. But he had successfully blocked the defendants’ efforts to have an international human rights expert testify, and from invoking the first amendment as a defense, on the grounds that the alleged conduct does not constitute protected speech.
Gonzalez, a sophomore at the time of the protest, is set to graduate this year but said he feels under scrutiny by university administrators.

“It’s difficult to go to classes and try to walk from your library to your classroom and get followed by campus security,” he said. “It feels demeaning, being surveilled to that degree … All I have done is stand up for what I believe in.”

articles.title: Colombia declares public calamity as wildfire threatens popular tourist area
articles.summary:
Wildfire forces evacuations and burns through mountains surrounding Villa de Leyva in the north-east

Colombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains…

blocks.text: Colombian authorities declared a public calamity as a wildfire burned through mountains surrounding one of the country’s best-known colonial towns in the north-east, scorching large swaths of vegetation and forcing evacuations.
Nearly 20 active fires are burning across the South American country. Dry conditions have increased fire danger in Colombia as it braces for the effects of El Niño, which can help wildfires spread.

The fire in Villa de Leyva, a popular tourist destination about 160km (100 miles) north-east of the capital, Bogotá, began Saturday on a mountain overlooking the town. By Sunday evening, authorities said about 290 hectares (717 acres) had been affected – an area roughly equivalent to 400 soccer fields – and the blaze was about 50% under control.

Strong winds have complicated efforts to contain the flames, which at times advanced toward populated areas. Local authorities declared an emergency, suspended in-person classes Monday and carried out preventive evacuations, including at hotels near the fire.

blocks.caption: Flames and smoke rise from a wildfire in Villa de Leyva, Colombia, on 20 September 2026.  Photograph: Sebastian Arguello/Reuters

blocks.text: More than 400 firefighters, emergency workers, residents and volunteers took part in the response, while four helicopters dropped water on the flames. Carlos Amaya, the governor of Boyaca, where Villa de Leyva is located, said aircraft carried out about 170 water drops Sunday, releasing 240,000 liters (63,400 gallons).

Fabio Arjona, Colombia’s environment minister, said preliminary information from the disaster management agency suggested it may have been deliberately started, but authorities were still investigating.
Abelardo de la Espriella, the Colombian president, said Sunday on X the Villa de Leyva fire was about 50% controlled and contained on the ground.

Colombia’s national disaster management agency said in its latest nationwide update that authorities were monitoring 27 forest fires, with 19 still active and eight under control. Nine of the active fires were in Tolima, a mountainous region south-west of Bogotá, while others were burning across several parts of the country’s Andean region.

The weather agency said last week that 279 municipalities were under some level of wildfire warning, including 36 under its highest, red-alert level, with much of the risk concentrated in the Andean and Caribbean regions.
Between 16 June 16 and 6 August, Colombia recorded 438 forest fires in 191 municipalities, affecting about 7,153 hectares of vegetation, according to government figures.

Neighboring Ecuador is also battling a wave of wildfires. Ecuador’s national risk management agency said Sunday that 12 fires remained active across the country, while more than 21,800 hectares of vegetation have burned so far this year.

High temperatures and strong winds have helped flames spread rapidly in some areas. A fire on the slopes of Ecuador’s Imbabura volcano burned about 300 hectares before being brought under control Sunday after three days of firefighting.
El Niño is a periodic warming of the tropical Pacific Ocean that can reduce rainfall and raise temperatures in parts of the country, creating conditions that allow wildfires to spread more easily.

Disaster officials have said the period of greatest risk across the region from the developing El Niño is expected between October and April, with wildfires and water shortages among the main concerns.

articles.title: US strikes on alleged drug boats may constitute ‘crimes against humanity’, UN finds
articles.summary:
Dozens of US attacks on boats in the Pacific and Caribbean have killed more than 230 people since September 2025

A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there…

blocks.text: A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean “constituted crimes against humanity”.

The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean.

The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further.

In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reported by the BBC, Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”.
He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.”

The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put the death toll at 234 people in 66 attacks.

US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”.

As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking.
Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”.
The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US.

“Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added.
The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment.

Although Trump recently claimed the bombings had stopped 97% of all illegal drugs entering the US by sea, according to available data, the attacks have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the US.

Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, were at best low-ranked participants in trafficking networks.

articles.title: Man and police officer wounded in exchange of gunfire near Ontario synagogue
articles.summary:
Officials say man was critically injured and officer was wounded in Yom Kippur incident near Belleville synagogue

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday…

blocks.text: A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.

The Canadian province’s special investigations unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles (160km) east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man at about 7.10pm and that both were taken to a hospital.

Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The special investigations unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.
Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was under way.
Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier, said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.

“I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people “have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear” and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
“My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones,” Ford said.
York regional police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Sunday’s shooting comes months after Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, warned that the country was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.

Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues, and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.

Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

articles.title: Pakistan jails sisters of Imran Khan before protest seeking his release
articles.summary:
Police crack down on family and political supporters of former PM who say authorities are ‘slowly killing’ him in prison

Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran…
articles.byline: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi

blocks.text: Three sisters of Pakistan’s incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan have been arrested amid a heavy-handed government crackdown on plans for a nationwide protest to demand Khan’s release.

The lawyer for the three sisters – Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi – said on Monday that they had all been detained and jailed for 30 days under a warrant that accused them of being a threat to public order.

Leaders from Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) condemned the “illegal harassment” of his sisters. Since Khan was arrested and held in prison on corruption charges in 2023, his sisters have been vocal advocates for his release.

His family and party allege that Khan is being kept in solitary confinement and has been denied visits and calls from his family for six months, as well as being allegedly prevented from accessing vital medical treatment for an eye condition.

The arrest of Khan’s sisters marked a dramatic escalation of a crackdown on PTI members and supporters in the run up to a nationwide demonstration due to be held on Sunday – described as a “long march” – to demand the release of Khan and to protest an alleged erosion of democracy and the constitution under the ruling coalition government.

Khan’s sisters hold a political position in PTI. Since protesting against their brother’s detention – including by camping outside the prison where he is held, demanding to see him – they have been named in various court cases. This is the first time they have all been held in prison.

Aleema was arrested in Lahore on Sunday as she was travelling to a private club; her driver was also picked up by police. Uzma and Noreen were then arrested at around 3am on Monday morning, after they held a press conference to condemn Aleema’s detention at her house in Lahore.

According to their lawyer, Rana Mudassir Umar, hundreds of police officers later surrounded the family home as more than 100 entered to arrest Uzma and Noreen, as well as their children, grandchildren – who are four and six years old – and the household staff. The house was raided and all their phones were taken.
By 7am on Monday morning, the children and grandchildren had been released but the three sisters were held and charged under the country’s Maintenance of Public Order law, according to Umar.
He said: “They have not been allowed any family access, no legal counsellor access and they were not even allowed to bring clothes or basic things.
“We have challenged their arrests in the high court in Lahore and [are] hoping we will get a hearing soon.”

While Pakistan is ostensibly ruled by a civilian coalition government, the army is widely regarded as the country’s most powerful establishment, led by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, who fell out with Khan while Khan was prime minister. The current government was brought to power in an election in 2024 which was widely documented as rigged, allegedly by military intervention, to prevent Khan’s party returning to power.

Speaking to the Guardian last week, Khan’s two sons, who are based in London and fighting for his release, accused Munir of a “personal vendetta” against their father and alleged the Pakistani authorities were “slowly killing” Khan in prison.
Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday taht the government would “find a permanent solution” to prevent to march going ahead and shutting down swathes of the country “once and for all”.

Despite Khan’s lengthy incarceration, he is still regarded as Pakistan’s most popular politician and there are fears among officials that large numbers could turn out to support PTI’s march on Sunday. It is being held as discontentment is rife on the streets amidst an economic crisis and crippling petrol shortages due to the turmoil in the Middle East and the Gulf. Disgust at the alleged mistreatment of Khan is also widespread.
Khan’s party has faced constant harassment over the past three years, with most senior PTI figures either in jail or pressed to leave politics.

Sheikh Waqas Akram, a senior PTI leader, said the government feared that hundreds of thousands of people may turn out to the long march and “topple the government”, as protest movements have done recently in neighbouring countries such as Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

Over the weekend, the capital of Pakistan, Islamabad, was transformed into a fortress of heavy security, with barriers and heavy armed security lining the roads and shipping containers placed to block the entrances into the city.

“Punjab police are raiding houses, harassing families, bulldozing houses and arresting workers and families,” Akram said. “They are going to insane levels to crush the long march and stop it with violence and arrests. This illegitimate government know they can’t survive if people are allowed to protest and march on Islamabad in huge numbers.”
