Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Published September 21, 2026last updated September 21, 2026
Ex-Transport Minister Scheuer goes on trial for perjury

blocks.caption: Plans for a highway toll (Maut) in Germany have so far failed Image: Bernd Wüstneck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A perjury trial against former Transport Minister Andreas Scheuer kicked off at the Berlin District Court on Monday.

Scheuer and his co-defendant Gerhard Schulz, a former state secretary, are accused of having lied to a parliamentary committee investigating a failed scheme some seven years ago to levy a highway toll on foreign motorists.
Both of them deny the charges made against them.
What are the charges against Scheuer and Schulz?

The two are accused of lying to the committee about having signed a contract with a company to run the toll operations despite knowing that the European Court of Justice (ICJ) was likely to declare the scheme illegal.

Scheur's Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party of the Christian Democrats (CDU) currently led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, had devised a plan to levy tolls on all drivers but then compensate German motorists by reducing their motor vehicle taxes.
The scheme was shot down in 2019 by the ICJ for breaching EU rules.
But by that time, the Transport Ministry under Scheuer had already signed binding contracts with the operators who were to be tasked with executing the plan.
The German government was then forced to pay €243 million ($283 million at current exchange rates) in damages to the companies involved.
Jail sentences possible
The trial is planned to take place over 12 days, with a verdict expected on November 25.
If found guilty, the accused could face jail sentences ranging from three months to five years.

articles.title: Germany's car crisis: Can the 35-hour workweek survive?
articles.summary: German carmakers want employees to work 40 hours instead of the current 35 without extra pay, arguing it would improve competitiveness. Unions strongly oppose the proposal and view it as an attack on…

image.caption: Germany's auto industry is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the countryImage: Jan Woitas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany's famed automotive sector is facing a deep crisis, squeezed by high manufacturing costs, punitive US tariffs, intensifying competition from China and a difficult transition to electric vehicles.
Industry heavyweights such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz and BMW have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.
The branch is shedding jobs faster than any other industrial sector in the country.

Volkswagen, for instance, is looking to cut about 15% of its workforce worldwide, or 100,000 jobs, by the end of the decade. BMW announced it will cut up to 8,000 jobs — about 5% of its workforce — by the end of 2027.
Auto suppliers such as Bosch and ZF Friedrichshafen have also announced thousands of job reductions amid tough market conditions and global competition.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?

Germany's automotive industry is losing competitiveness as costs rise and production shifts abroad, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, director of the Center for Automotive Research (CAR) in the German city of Bochum.
"In 2018, the industry employed around 830,000 people. Currently, that number is below 700,000," he told DW. "We project that by around 2030, it will be 500,000."

Regaining competitiveness and securing jobs in the future will require an array of measures including lower production and energy costs, better logistics infrastructure and favorable tax conditions, he added.
Labor costs too high in Germany?
Auto industry executives agree that labor costs in Germany are too high compared to international rivals.
Labor costs in the country average $3,307 (€2,882) per vehicle, compared to $769 in Japan and $597 in China, according to a reportpublished by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman.
To trim labor costs, carmakers want employees in Germany to work 40 hours a week instead of the current 35 hours, without any increase in pay.
The 35-hour workweek has long been standard across much of Germany's automotive industry, having emerged from collective bargaining agreements negotiated in the 1980s and 1990s.
It reflects an era when Germany was highly competitive, said Dudenhöffer, adding: "That time is over."
Workers' unions, however, vehemently oppose longer working hours.

Christiane Benner, the head of the influential IG Metall trade union, said workers had already accepted wage cuts and other concessions worth several billion euros, yet were now being told that this was still not enough.

The union argues that German automakers are struggling with weak demand and underutilized factories, not a shortage of labor hours. "Not a single additional car will be sold just because the workforce works longer hours," the union announced.
IG Metall is holding demonstrations at more than 200 locations nationwide on September 21 to oppose job cuts and other measures affecting working conditions in the automotive sector.
VW is bringing out the axe
Can longer working hours save jobs?
The union is "fighting for relics from 20 years ago, forgetting today's reality," Dudenhöffer said.
The expert estimated that if carmakers were to move from a 35-hour week to a 40-hour week, personnel costs would decrease by 13%.
"We wouldn't be taking money away from employees, but we would be creating conditions that would make jobs possible in Germany, in the automotive industry, in the future," he underlined.

Stefan Bratzel, head of the Center of Automotive Management (CAM) in Bergisch Gladbach, said the 35-hour week represents a key achievement for trade unions in their collective bargaining history, so "conflict is inevitable" between management and unions.
On the other hand, more working hours for the same pay would mathematically lower labor costs per hour, he added.
"Ultimately, this raises the question of how the burdens of the current transformation are to be distributed between companies and employees," said Bratzel.
How can Germany's auto industry recover?
Experts say improving labor costs at German production sites is necessary, but it alone will not solve the industry's deeper structural problems.
"Working five hours more per week alone will not win the technological race against China," said Bratzel.

He stressed that, to restore their competitive edge, German carmakers need to deliver attractive and affordable electric vehicles, invest heavily in software and AI, and improve the efficiency of their development and manufacturing processes.
"German manufacturers must be at least as innovative and high-performing in technological terms as they are expensive by international standards," said Bratzel.
At the same time, he explained, Germany requires competitive framework conditions regarding energy, taxes, bureaucracy and infrastructure.
Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production?
Dudenhöffer echoed this view, saying that Germany must pursue difficult but necessary reforms.
"Germany can only be considered a viable option for its automotive industry and jobs if we regain our competitiveness," he said.
And for that, action is required on multiple fronts, including lowering labor and energy costs, adjusting taxes, and creating better logistics infrastructure, he added.

"But the coming years will be very tough," Dudenhöffer warned. "And they will become even tougher if we stick to the status quo and believe we can simply rest on the prosperity we enjoyed 20 years ago."

articles.title: 'No surprises' as results emerge in Russian parliamentary election
articles.summary: Preliminary results suggest that Kremlin-backed United Russia is on course to retain its constitutional majority.

blocks.text: Preliminary results from Russia's elections suggest that the party backed by President Vladimir Putin, United Russia, will maintain its grip on parliament.
The outcome comes as no surprise, according to the BBC's Russia editor, Steve Rosenberg, who has been following the elections from Moscow.
The vote comes after more than four and a half years of war against Ukraine, a conflict which has seen huge battlefield losses for the Russian army and sparked economic hardship.
The only anti-war party, Yabloko, was removed the ballot in the run-up to polling day – although some candidates remained in some constituencies.

articles.title: Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals
articles.summary: After a plane journey in shackles, an Iranian woman found herself in the middle of Africa in a country she did not know existed. She is one of thousands deported from the US on the back of shadowy…

blocks.text: Nika’s story

blocks.caption: Silhouette of an Iranian woman, DHS officers wrestle a detainee to the ground

blocks.text: No one would tell the shackled detainees onboard the US immigration plane where they were going. The officers in charge would taunt them when they asked, they said. It was only when the seat-back video screens finally showed a map that the 18 migrants worked it out.
Their destination was Central African Republic (CAR), a country few of them had even heard of.

Nika, a 32-year-old Iranian woman, recalled how the handcuffs dug into her wrists. She begged the officers to loosen them, but they did not. Other passengers had it worse, she said. Some of the men were restrained in black and yellow body wraps, as if mummified, after resisting orders to get on the plane.

Nika, who had fled Iran 18 months earlier after protesting against its regime, had imagined the US as a place of sanctuary. Iran was already one of the most repressive countries in the world when she left, and its horrors had only deepened since then: security forces gunned down thousands of other demonstrators this year, then Donald Trump’s administration launched the war there.

After more than a year locked up in a US immigration detention centre, Nika, whose name the Guardian has changed to protect her family in Iran, was granted legal protections and freed on a judge’s orders. Within two weeks, the Department of Homeland Security had rearrested her, and days later she was on the plane heading 7,000 miles east.
“They never told me they were going to deport me [to] this country,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t know anything about Africa.”

The Department of State warns US citizens not to travel to CAR because it says it is too dangerous. Nika spends most of her days there under a form of self-imprisonment, too scared to venture out from her small bedroom as she waits for an answer to the question on which her life depends: will she be sent back to Iran, and to a regime that could kill her?

Nika is one of more than 25,000 people deported by the Trump administration to countries that are not their own. About 20,000 people have been bussed to Mexico, according to a count by Refugees International and Human Rights First. And more than 5,000 others have been put on flights to countries in Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and central Asia to which they have no connection, and then, often, returned to the countries where US immigration judges had ruled their lives or liberty were at risk.

Human rights lawyers describe these so-called third-country national arrangements as part of a “show of force” by the US intended to discourage migrants and asylum seekers from entering. People from Peru and Colombia have been sent to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). On 20 August, four Cubans, a Brazilian and a Cameroonian refused to disembark in Liberia, and were sent to Equatorial Guinea instead.

In order to compile the most comprehensive account of a policy that has mostly operated behind closed doors, the Guardian joined 23 other media organisations in the Deportation Project, a joint investigation coordinated by Paris-based Forbidden Stories. The consortium interviewed more than 100 people affected by, or involved in, the US drive to extinguish unauthorised immigration, and reviewed documents outlining details of the agreements made by US officials with governments around the world.

It has tracked more than 100 flights that have carried migrants and asylum seekers to 28 different countries. This is likely to be an undercount as the consortium’s dataset only includes flights it was able to independently verify.

The pace of flights is increasing. After an initial wave during the opening months of the second Trump administration, the number of deportations spiked in August again when, according to a count by Human Rights First, a record 16 flights carried people to 13 different countries that were not their own.

A US federal appeals court ruled on Friday that third-country removals were unlawful, arguing that they violated due process because people are not notified with enough time to mount a legal challenge to the decision to send them to another country. Human rights lawyers suggested this should immediately ground third-country deportation flights. The government is expected to appeal against the judgment, and to press ahead with its policy.

A state department spokesperson said implementing the Trump administration’s immigration policies was a “top priority” and “we are unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”. They added: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The Trump administration has said the people it deports are criminals. Yet documents obtained by the Washington Post as part of this project show that a majority of the 35 countries that have signed deals with the US have said they will not accept migrants with violent criminal records.
The people forced on to planes include those who spent most of their lives in the US, parents detained on the school run, the adult children of elderly relatives who depend on them for care.

Many are people whose fear of returning home was deemed so credible that immigration judges barred their removal from the US. Nika had been granted “withholding of removal”, a protection for individuals who may face severe harm in their country of origin but are ineligible for asylum. On 28 May, not only was she released from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s custody, but she was eligible to find a job, to work, and to stay.
The rug pull

blocks.caption: Trump’s deportation drive is being led by Stephen Miller (left)

blocks.text: Nika’s lawyer, Sahar Jalili, is Iranian and, like her client, studied in Tehran. She took the case when she was pregnant, and often worked past the point of exhaustion. “That could be me,” she said of Nika.

Combing through the case file, Jalili was shocked to learn ICE had officially decided to send Nika to CAR’s capital, Bangui, just eight days before a judge ordered her release from the detention centre. Her uncle’s family had prepared a room for her in Los Angeles. It took her two days to get there, and she spent a week with them, unfurling, after 18 months of hell.
Her re-arrest on 8 June, during what ICE officers had presented as a routine check-in, felt like cruelty for cruelty’s sake, Jalili said.
Nika said she had finished her appointment and left when an officer called her uncle and asked him to drive her back to pick up some papers.

This time there were new questions. A man took Nika’s fingerprints, then her photograph, Jalili said. “Then he came back accompanied by a female ICE officer, and they said put your hands above your head.” She said she was arrested, handcuffed and led to the basement.

Nika felt numb, she said, as she was transferred out of the detention facility that evening. Anti-ICE demonstrators smacked their palms on the side of the van as she passed through protests that had become a regular feature in LA.

For Jalili, the previous two days had already been a blur, as she and her colleagues battled to save two other Iranian women from being put on the same plane for Bangui. The lawyers managed to get the other two women off the plane, but not Nika. The only difference between them was that Nika was detained last, so by the time a network of immigration lawyers had learned of her case, there was not enough time before the flight departed.

Jalili said she begged every ICE officer: “Give me two days. Just two days.” She recalled: “They told me that they had respected the judge’s order to release her. But they’d never promised not to send her to a third country.”
African deals

blocks.caption: Montage of images, including one of Rabbiatu Kuyateh, government papers and maps

blocks.text: When Rabbiatu Kuyateh, 58, learned that the country she had been sent to, Ghana, was deporting her to her childhood homeland, she was so scared it took a scrum of people to force her into the waiting van.

A video captured the moment last November when she was dragged, shoeless and distraught, by her hair. She still remembers the crack of her head on the stone steps as she begged not to be returned to Sierra Leone, screaming: “I’m not going”.

blocks.caption: Rabbiatu Kuyateh being forcibly removed from her temporary accommodation in Ghana

blocks.text: Kuyateh was a nurse and had spent most of her life in the US with her parents, after fleeing Sierra Leone. She cared for American coronavirus patients during the pandemic and had looked after disabled adults and children in the years since.

She had scrapped hard for the life she built, she said. She had raised her son, Mohamed, alone and they had bought a house together. By the time Trump was re-elected in 2024, her parents were so frail she began each day by checking on them before her shift, and then returning to make sure they were ready for bed.
In order to accelerate its expulsion of people such as Kuyateh, the Trump administration has remade the very institutions that were once intended to protect migrants who fled persecution.

“I would describe [this] as the Trump administration’s way of trying to undermine the concept of asylum and refugee protection,” said Alma David, one of the leading immigration lawyers tracking the policy. “While the US understands that they can’t deport them to their home country legally, what they can do is basically send them through this third country that perceives itself as a transit hub.”

The drive is being led by Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, who has been open about his desire to end most migration to the US. In interviews with the Washington Post as part of the Deportation Project, current and former US officials said Miller had rolled out the third-country removals policy by pushing key appointments inside the state department that have allowed him to overrule other foreign policy objectives in service of his agenda.

Among them is Christian Ehrhardt, a career state department official who heads the newly formed Office of Remigration – its name incorporating a term adopted by the far right to describe the forcible expulsion of minority ethnic immigrants. Ehrhardt has helped secure at least 13 third-country deportation agreements in Africa, after diplomatic tours through the continent.

Internal records reviewed by the Washington Post show the Trump administration has pledged at least $410m (£307m) to secure such agreements with 38 different countries, almost a third of them in Africa.

They indicate that $30m was earmarked for Cameroon, in order to support UN operations in the country, in return for accepting 1,000 migrants. The US has so far sent only 44. The DRC was promised $75m towards UN operations there, in return for accepting 2,000 migrants. It has only received 15, and flights to Kinshasa are on hold due to the country’s Ebola outbreak.

The arrangements differ from country to country. A handful, including Eswatini, have agreed to accept people with violent criminal histories. But many have said they will not take anyone with a record of violence or other types of serious crimes. The state department did not respond to questions about details of these agreements.

Ghana will only take people from west Africa; CAR did not specify nationalities, and the passengers on Nika’s plane were from places including Afghanistan, Iraq and Kyrgyzstan. Most of them had no ties to Africa at all, she said.

On 1 July 2025, Kuyateh’s son, Mohamed, had accompanied her to a routine ICE check-in, as her immigration status required. He remembered his mother feeling anxious that the cuffs on an officer’s belt were for her. “I doubt it,” Mohamed told her. But when they called Kuyateh into an interrogation room, he was told to wait outside.
“That’s the last time I saw her,” he said.

During Kuyateh’s four months in ICE custody, Mohamed spoke to her often. He had not heard from her on the day in November when he said he was called by another detainee who told him she had been sent to Texas. “And I was just like, why is she going to Texas?”
Two days later Kuyateh called him in tears. She was in Ghana, about to be sent to Sierra Leone.

The footage of her being dragged into a bus, beginning the onward deportation, appeared to anger the Ghanaian authorities when it spread across social media, according to Malick, the Senegalese man, also deported from the US, who filmed it. The Guardian has given him a pseudonym out of concern for his safety. “They got angry,” Malick said. “They came in the evening, at night, with two trucks full of soldiers.”

He said the troops drove his group to a remote military camp with faltering electricity and little contact with the outside world. The Ghanaian government did not respond to questions from the Guardian.

One woman sent to the camp said she grew so scared of what might happen if she was returned to her native Senegal that she attempted suicide by drinking bleach. She was treated in hospital, then sent back to Senegal anyway. “I drank the bleach because I wanted to die,” she said. “Because they wanted to force me to go back to my country.”
Malaria

blocks.caption: Montage of images including one of a man in handcuffs and one of a persons hand in a hospital bed

blocks.text: Onboard Nika’s flight on 11 June this year, the inflight video showed Ghana as its initial destination, so the passengers assumed that was where they were going. But their stop in the capital, Accra, was brief. The 18 passengers then landed in Bangui at 9.45pm, flight monitors said. The officers onboard removed their cuffs, but did not get off the plane.

blocks.caption: Deportation plane arriving in Bangui on 11 June

blocks.text: For several hours, the group did not meet anyone who spoke English. “They were communicating with hand gestures, like, get on a bus, and then they put us on a bus. And then they took us to give us some vaccinations, and I didn’t know what they were going to inject me with,” Nika said. It turned out to be for yellow fever.
Her room was in an apartment block. She was told she could stay for three months. But the idea of returning to Iran was unfathomable.

US-based Iranian rights groups say they have been unable to determine the fates of hundreds of other Iranian nationals deported back home during the course of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A recent lawsuit filed against ICE alleges the administration has shared the records of Iranian asylum-seekers with the very regime they had fled, further elevating the risk for those sent back.

When a headache started clouding her brain, Nika thought it was a migraine. She felt sick, her body hurt. She had been bitten by so many mosquitoes that her skin looked bruised, she said. A medical report, seen by the Guardian, confirmed she had malaria. Speaking by phone, Nika said: “I didn’t even know what that was.”

Back in Los Angeles, Jalili waited anxiously on updates about Nika’s situation. There were injections every 12 hours to clear her bloodstream of parasites. The bad news did not stop when she was well enough to return to her accommodation. Jalili was horrified to learn Nika had been deported from the US without her passport, meaning she had neither identification documents, nor a visa, and on trips to the hospital and vegetable market, police officers used her lack of papers to make threats.
The CAR government did not respond to a request for comment.
The second time she was stopped, Nika said, the police officer mimed the action of putting cuffs on her. The message, she said, was: “I can take you in, unless you pay us.”

blocks.caption: Montage of images including a cityscape and a woman silhouetted against a window

blocks.text: As the Trump administration accelerates its third-country deportations, CAR is one of 13 host countries where the deported are being supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), a UN agency, which provides them with food, lodgings and psychological counsel upon their arrival.
Although the Trump administration has announced sweeping cuts to its funding for UN agencies, there seem to be exceptions where the funds enable this deportation programme.

In March last year, the state department spelled out the logic. From now on, it said, humanitarian funding would be used to “reduce mass and illegal immigration, such as funding voluntary returns of illegal aliens, incentivising governments to implement safe third-country agreements, and building the migration management capacity of other countries”.

According to a federal government database that tracks spending, more than 60% of US grants to the IOM during the second Trump administration have gone to programmes in countries that accept deported migrants. In CAR, that meant an allocation of $85m. The highest US contribution to IOM in CAR under the Biden administration, according to the database, was $14m.

Nika said she had been treated well by the agency. “The people here are doing their best,” she said. The accommodation was secure and transport was provided when needed. “But at the same time, it’s not living. I’m breathing here, I’m not dying. But I can’t leave the house without a driver they provide here. I can’t find jobs. I don’t speak their language.”

The potential for a negative perception of its involvement in the programme is something the IOM has grappled with. An internal risk assessment for a programme supporting third-country nationals sent from the US to one African country, seen by the Guardian, warns it could lead the agency to be “perceived as complicit”.

An IOM spokesperson said in a statement that such assessments were conducted in order to ascertain whether host nations were able to commit to safeguards for the migrants, but added: “We are fully cognisant that states use financial assistance to advance their national priorities. However, IOM’s decisions to accept funding, provide post-arrival assistance, or support assisted voluntary return are guided by our own mandate and principles, and rest on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does.”
Many in the human rights field are uncomfortable the UN is easing the process for governments that agree to cooperate with the Trump administration.

“It just feels very incongruous for IOM to be the organisation in charge of these men and women,” said Alma David. “These aren’t migrants in your typical sense. These aren’t people who chose to migrate,” she said. “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.”
Life in the shadows

blocks.caption: Montage of images, including of a woman and a man and official US documents

blocks.text: People who had been returned from third countries to the places they were born describe a life now lived in the shadows. Kuyateh left Sierra Leone within days of being sent back there. The Guardian is not naming her location. “I don’t sleep at night,” she said. “Sometimes I just wake up. I’ll be sitting down like, what am I doing here? Why am I here?”

She called her family every day. Sometimes, she said, she felt too sad to turn on the video and see their faces. She could get through the conversation with her mother without tears, she said, “but whenever I talk to my daddy, I’ll be crying. And when I sit here, I think about them. It hurts so much.”
She was not sure what scared her more: the thought of dying alone in a foreign country, or knowing that her parents might die without her at their bedside.

Annan, a gay man who fled Ghana after he was outed, and then hunted, by members of his family, said he was terrified when he touched back down in Accra. He had refused to disembark during his initial deportation from the US to Sierra Leone, and had to be forcibly removed from the plane, he said. He later begged authorities not to return him, he said, but they did not listen.

In a statement, the Sierra Leonean government said it took its “international obligations seriously” but that questions relating to immigration protections afforded by an American court were for the US government to address.

It added: “So far, no individual returned to Sierra Leone under the TCNA [third-country national arrangement] has requested to remain in Sierra Leone or not to be returned to his or her country of choice either in west Africa or beyond.”
Annan’s mother had used her savings to pay for his escape to the US. She was distraught when he called to say he was back. “She knew she couldn’t protect me,” he said.

He shared footage of where he lived now: an abandoned building with no electricity or running water in a neighbouring country, he said. He spent his daylight hours hiding, and walked almost an hour to find food when darkness fell. His bed was a blanket on the floor, although he barely slept, he said, too scared of being infected by one of the insects that crawled or buzzed around him. He said the loneliness felt crippling.

In recent weeks, someone had texted him anonymously, saying that his survival, as a gay man, would not be tolerated. The message made him feel hopeless: he could run, it said, but he could not hide for ever.
Exhaustion

blocks.caption: Montage of images including men walking towards a plane and people sitting in a large room

blocks.text: In Los Angeles, Jalili is getting more calls about clients bound for deportation flights. In June, a 30-year-old Iranian woman with a blood disorder that made her so weak she needed a walker was told she would be sent to the landlocked south African nation of Eswatini.
Another client was “going crazy”, Jalili said. “They’re coming up with a new country for her every week.”

Immigration lawyers said that while their jobs had always been hard, the scale of the efforts to obstruct those opposing the Trump administration’s drive to quash all types of irregular migration was unprecedented.

When a client is detained, avenues of accountability have largely been shut, including the office of an independent ombudsman for immigration detention, which was responsible for investigating abuses and misconduct.

In court, immigration lawyers can face hostile judges after the Trump administration purged some of those deemed insufficiently loyal to the deportation agenda. Meanwhile, the cost of even filing a case has risen steeply, under the terms of a bill passed through Congress in July last year.

Jalili, like many others, spent much of the first Trump administration mounting legal challenges against a policy of separating children from their parents at the US-Mexico border. Knowing that what would follow might be worse, she decided on the eve of Trump’s re-election to start her own firm to fight the coming storm
It was not uncommon for calls from the desperate families of new ICE detainees to wake her in the night.
One of the biggest challenges, said Erica Reilly, an immigration attorney based in Washington DC, was basic communication with ICE officers.

“You send all these emails to deportation officers, and you’re like: ‘Hi, just following up again on the email I sent you last week, and the week before that, and the week before that, and the week before that, that you haven’t responded to,’” she said. “And they know they don’t have to because there’s no accountability.”
The worst thing, she said, was the powerlessness. But the cruelty and the lack of access, she had come to believe, “that’s all the point”.
“I think that the administration is doing what they can to get enough people to say, well, the alternative is too scary or too uncertain or too bad. I’ll just leave on my own.”
Getting through the day meant reformulating the wins, Reilly said. “Getting a call back from a deportation officer shouldn’t be a win, but in this environment it is.”

Jalili said she did her best to focus on the battles she could win. When she heard Nika’s flight had left for Bangui, she sank to the floor, called her mother, and began to cry. “It’s not a situation where you can just say: ‘Oh, I did my best.’”
Nika had lost the life she knew in Iran. The US offered little better. Jalili listed the cost.

“Being detained for 17 months. Being released from the federal judge’s order for 10 days. Being stripped away from her uncle’s hands. Being put in a car and then on a flight in shackles, and for 24 hours, sitting on that flight. She must have felt so lonely.”
Additional reporting by Alice Speri

articles.title: Macron and Carney announce closer France-Canada ties amid Trump tensions
articles.summary:
Two leaders meet in French territory off Canada as Ottawa seeks stronger relations with EU while fighting trade war with US

The leaders of France and Canada have pledged closer ties to…

blocks.text: The leaders of France and Canada have pledged closer ties to grapple with rising geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values, after ⁠they met in a ⁠French territory off Canada’s Atlantic coast.

The two leaders’ visit to Saint-Pierre ​and Miquelon – the first by a French president since 2014 and the first by a Canadian prime minister – came just weeks ⁠after Donald Trump posted an image showing the islands, as well as all of Canada and other countries in North America, covered by the US flag.
Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the ⁠EU amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war with the US.

“Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate ​change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to ‌our sovereignty,” Canada’s Mark Carney said in a statement ‌alongside France’s Emmanuel Macron on Sunday. “The time has come to strengthen our ties.”
Macron added that the two allies agreed to forge closer ties in sectors ranging ‌from space and climate to energy.

“We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions, and the strategic autonomy that we defend,” the French president said.
Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual UN general assembly of world leaders, had a symbolic weight following Trump’s social media post.

The image Trump shared showed the US flag draped over a map of the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, and was labelled “United States of America”. It included Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories.

Responding to questions on Trump’s post, Macron dismissed any notion that the territories ​could not be French and said he did not need to reaffirm that point every day just because “people have strange ideas or say strange things”.
For France, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic.
The territory also occupies a key place in France’s cooperation with Canada, including over energy.
Macron, whose government is facing increased pressure at home over rising fuel ⁠prices, said the talks had opened the door for bilateral discussions aimed at sealing concrete deals. ​
Paris hopes Canada will broaden its exports of ​liquefied natural gas to Europe rather than primarily ​to Asia.
“Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,” Macron said.
The two leaders ​also discussed Canada’s relationship with the ‌EU after the bloc ​proposed ​that Ottawa become its first associate member, something Macron said France supported.
Trump threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” and a halt to trade after the proposal – an idea he derided as “laughable”.

Any move towards deeper integration is likely to face hurdles. More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

articles.title: German state elections deal a blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz
articles.summary: Elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have dealt the CDU a historic defeat while the AfD saw a massive gain. The pressure on Germany's unpopular chancellor is mounting.

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) is coming under even greater pressure due to his party's election defeats in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western PomeraniaImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two of Germany's 16 federal states, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, have just elected new state legislatures. The results for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) represent yet another major blow in turbulent times both nationally and internationally.
In northeastern Germany, projections suggest that the CDU narrowly failed to clear the 5% threshold for representation in parliament, a historic first in the party's history.
In the German capital, the party that led the state government, lost nearly a third of its support, dropping to around 20%.

Just minutes after the first projections were released, Merz made a statement: "We can't sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — it was a disaster." As for the heavy losses in Berlin, he described the outcome there as "reasonable."

For the CDU, this marks the third electoral defeat in two weeks. In the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, the party came in far behind the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which the Office for the Protection of the Constitution has classified as partially far-right extremist.
In the wake of this debacle, Merz, whose term began in 2025, appeared visibly shaken.
German Chancellor Merz vows to push ahead with reforms
At the federal level, Merz governs in coalition with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), which saw mixed results in Sunday's state elections.

With around 36% of the vote, SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig — who has been in office since 2017 — finished just behind the far-right AfD in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD, on the other hand, nearly doubled its share of the vote compared to state elections in 2021, coming in first at 38%.
In Berlin, however, the SPD's share of the vote fell by a third to 12%, while the AfD became the third-largest party, winning 16% of the vote.

Meanwhile, the new frontrunner in the German capital is the socialist Left Party, with about 25%. It too was able to double its share of the vote, just as the AfD did in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. With the support of the SPD and the environmentalist Greens, the socialists — whom the CDU has labeled radical leftists and antisemites — would be able to form a coalition.
Berlin set to get a left-wing mayor

If this happens, Elif Eralp would be the first person from the Left Party to serve as mayor of Berlin. Leading up to the election, Eralp, the daughter of Turkish exiles, shared her vision in an interview with DW: "My vision for Berlin is an affordable Berlin where everyone — regardless of their background, religion, language or income — can lead a good life in dignity," Eralp said.
In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a coalition of SPD, the Left Party and the Greens is the most likely outcome. State Premier Schwesig said she was committed to a "stable democratic government."

Meanwhile, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel once again declared on election night that the CDU's containment strategy of refusing to cooperate with her party had failed. Speaking on the public television network ZDF, she said: "Our long-term goal, of course, is to hold coalition talks with the CDU."
Alice Weidel: Merz 'can no longer stay in office'
The AfD and the Left Party are stronger than the CDU and SPD

Both election results reflect widespread dissatisfaction among the population with Chancellor Merz and the coalition he leads with the SPD. In nationwide opinion polls, the governing coalition no longer has a majority. Here, too, the AfD is clearly in the lead, while the SPD is only narrowly ahead of the Left Party.

Parties on the political fringes are now gaining significantly more support at both the federal and state levels than the ruling parties, which are frequently embroiled in arguments on the federal level. These disputes often arise in connection with the reform agenda announced months ago by Chancellor Merz, aimed at bringing the rapidly rising costs of health, long-term care and pension insurance under control.

Despite yet another election setback, the German chancellor intends to stay the course: "The reforms must go ahead. Of course, this puts us all in a difficult situation. But we will shoulder this responsibility. I will shoulder this responsibility," he said.

After lengthy discussions, the coalition had already reached an agreement on health care reforms. Many things, like drugs and dental prosthetics, will become more expensive, while family insurance coverage will also be scaled back. These are all measures that won't win any new support for the already unpopular government. The same goes for the ongoing debate over reforms to the pension system, which is set to be supplemented by increased private retirement savings.
'I want to move our country forward'

Merz acknowledged that these changes would bring burdens and new uncertainties for many people. Nevertheless, he remained confident: "I want to move our country forward. I am also firmly convinced that the success of our reforms will not only improve our society but also boost our self-image and our image in the world."

In foreign policy as well, Merz — and with him the federal government — is coming under increasing pressure as a result of the election results in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The AfD, which is particularly strong in eastern Germany, opposes military support for Ukraine in its fight against Russia's invasion.
'What needs to be done now requires backbone, resolve and patience'

This complex situation makes things even more difficult for the federal government — and Merz is well aware of this. Taking stock of the heavy election defeats suffered by his CDU, he said: "What needs to be done now requires backbone, resolve and patience. I will muster that — as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as the chancellor of our country."
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Confused by what's going on in B.C. politics? Here's a timeline to catch you up

image.caption: Former B.C. United Leader Kevin Falcon, left, and former B.C. Conservative leaders Kerry-Lynne Findlay and John Rustad, have all failed to unite factions of B.C.'s centre-right voters under a single umbrella. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press; Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press; Emily Fagan/CBC)

blocks.text: If you haven't been paying close attention to B.C. politics, you may find yourself confused by recent news.

Just two years after the B.C. Conservatives nearly formed government, the party is in disarray, prompting speculation that the NDP government may hold a snap election in order to capitalize on the turmoil.
If that happens there will be new leaders, new parties and new decisions to make about who should lead the province.
Here's a brief timeline to get you up to date.
2022-24: The rise of the B.C. Conservatives
What's behind the surge in support for the B.C. Conservatives?

Since 1991, two parties have dominated B.C. politics: the B.C. Liberals, and the B.C. NDP. Right now, the NDP is in government, and has been since 2017. Prior to that the B.C. Liberals were in government for more than a decade, from 2001 to 2017, and were viewed as the most likely party to win back power from the NDP.
Though they share a name with the federal Liberals, the B.C. Liberals are actually not formally connected to their counterparts in Ottawa.

Instead, the party broadly served as a space where centre-right voters could coalesce, while the Conservative Party of British Columbia (also unaffiliated with their federal counterparts) spent the 1990s, 2000s and 2010s in the political wilderness, failing to win any seats in Victoria.
But that started to change in 2022 when John Rustad, a former B.C. Liberal cabinet minister, was kicked out of the party by leader Kevin Falcon over social media posts questioning climate science.

Rustad first sat as an Independent, but in February 2023 announced he had joined the Conservatives, giving the party their first seat in the Legislature in decades. In March, he was acclaimed as the party's new leader.

items: Longtime B.C. Liberal MLA removed from caucus after questioning climate change science

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the B.C. Liberal brand was dropping in public opinion polls — and in April 2023, 80 per cent of the party's members voted in favour of changing their name to B.C. United.
This was a time when the federal Liberal Party, under then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, was tanking in public opinion polls — and the federal Conservatives, under Pierre Poilievre, were soaring.
Are B.C. voters confused by new provincial party names?

Despite the lack of formal connections, the positive connotations of the Conservative name among many voters helped bolster Rustad's party's brand, and in September 2023, he was joined by former B.C. Liberal MLA Bruce Banman, giving the Conservatives official party status.
Their popularity continued to grow, and in August 2024, Falcon officially ended his party's campaign to form government in the Oct. 19 provincial election, throwing his support behind Rustad.
B.C. United Leader Kevin Falcon withdraws party from provincial election
That decision led to many longtime politicians within B.C. United, including former cabinet ministers, without a party to support them in their re-election campaigns.
While a handful made the jump to the Conservatives, many more either pulled out of the race or ran, and lost, as Independents.
When the final tally of votes were complete, the NDP had managed to hold onto government, with the Conservatives very close runners-up.
2025: Party deflections to the left and right
MLA Dallas Brodie expelled from B.C. Conservative caucus
Despite their electoral success, the B.C. Conservatives did not stay united for long.
In March 2025, Rustad removed MLA Dallas Brodie from the caucus for comments she made on a podcast which he characterized as mocking residential school survivors.

Her removal was followed by the immediate defection of two other MLAs, Jordan Kealy and Tara Armstrong, from the Conservatives — with Armstrong and Brodie going on to form yet another new political party, OneBC, while Kealy stayed Independent.

items: 2 MLAs defect from B.C. Conservative Party following Dallas Brodie's ouster

blocks.text: OneBC officially gained party status a few months later, and then lost it again in December when Armstrong said she no longer had confidence in Brodie's leadership, forcing her out of the role.
As it stands, Brodie is once again party leader, though OneBC does not have official party status. Armstrong remains an Independent.
OneBC ousts MLA Dallas Brodie as its leader — but she says she's fighting back
Meanwhile, tensions continued within the Conservative caucus, and in September 2025, MLA Elenore Sturko was removed from the party.
Sturko told reporters "socially liberal beliefs" had been silenced by the party.
A month later, MLA Amelia Boultbee also quit the party, citing Rustad's leadership. She would later join the NDP.

Concurrently, Rustad admitted to searching the phones of party MLAs, saying he was looking for leaks within the caucus. Despite the defections and controversy, Rustad survived a leadership review in September. But that survival wouldn't last.
2025-26: Rustad removed, Findlay falls
Rustad officially ceased being leader of the party he'd led out of the electoral wilderness on Dec. 4, 2025, citing concerns that trying to stay in power would lead to a "civil war."
His decision came after his party's board already said he'd been removed, and after 20 of the caucus's 39 members signed a letter saying they'd "lost confidence" in his leadership.
Rustad officially out as B.C. Conservative Party leader
This was followed by a new leadership race, which culminated with Kerry-Lynne Findlay taking the party reins in May 2026.
A former federal MP under Stephen Harper, Findlay promised a future Conservative government would emphasize "faith, family, and freedom," and to focus on removing the NDP from government.

Around the same time, Mike Bernier — one of the former B.C. Liberals ousted from politics by Rustad's rise — became leader of CentreBC, which promised to offer a middle ground between the NDP and Conservatives.
Kerry-Lynne Findlay named new B.C. Conservative leader
A few months later, on Aug. 14, a new round of resignations was kicked off when former finance critic Peter Milobar left the B.C. Conservative caucus to sit as an Independent.
He was followed by Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day, Banman and Áʼa꞉líya Warbus before the end of the month.

items: Calls for unity after wave of exits from B.C. Conservatives

blocks.text: September saw the bleeding continue — with Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis joining the exodus.
On Sept. 18, several of those MLAs announced they had joined CentreBC, and Bernier said he was stepping aside in order to let Milobar become leader.
Centrists, former B.C. Conservatives join forces under Peter Milobar-led CentreBC party
Findlay, however, vowed to stay on even as more people were forced from the Conservatives — including Trevor Halford, Claire Rattée and Rustad himself.
Then on Sunday, Sept. 20, MLA Linda Hepner left the Conservatives and shortly afterward, Findlay announced she would be stepping down.
Where we are now
With the opposition in turmoil, speculation is high that the B.C. NDP may use the opportunity to go to the polls while their primary opposition is in disarray.
So far, Premier David Eby has simply said the ruling NDP needs to be "election ready."
Why David Eby is considering a snap election

On Monday, Lorne Doerksen was announced as the interim Conservative party leader, and said that Rustad, Halford, Hepner, McInnis and Rattée had all been readmitted back into the Conservative Party caucus.
Of other former B.C. Conservatives still in the legislature, eight have said they are in in CentreBC: Milobar, Banman, Bird, Paton, Sturko, Warbus, Wat and Wilson.
Boultbee remains with the NDP, Brodie is listed as the leader of OneBC, and Amstrong is an Independent.
Also Independent is Richmond MLA Hon Chan, who was removed from the Conservative caucus in March after being charged with assault, to which he has pled not guilty.
After indicating he may rejoin the party under Findlay, Kealy stayed Independent after he was charged with sexual assault, a charge which he denies. Court proceedings are ongoing in both those cases.
The B.C. Green Party would also be a factor in the next election, with leader Emily Lowan potentially leading her first campaign.
The 26-year-old was elected party leader last year and has yet to win a seat in the Legislature, instead focusing her time on building party support throughout the province.
Lowan has said an early election call would smack of political opportunism.

articles.title: 3 MLAs, including former leader, returning to B.C. Conservative caucus as prospect of election looms

image.caption: John Rustad, former leader of the B.C. Conservative Party, says he has accepted an invite to rejoin the party after being expelled three days ago. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: Interim B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson is moving to repair ruptures in the Opposition that saw 13 legislators quit caucus or be expelled by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who stepped down on Sunday.
Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford and MLA Scott McInnis all say they've accepted invitations from Doerkson to rejoin the troubled caucus.
Rustad says in a statement that his "time as leader is over" but not his service to the province.
The Nechako Lakes MLA also says "high level" unity talks are underway between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party, and rated the chance of success at 95 per cent.

items: Lorne Doerkson named B.C. Conservatives interim leader following Findlay resignation

blocks.text: The developments come after the caucus of B.C.'s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay's resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.
An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad says there is a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were "obviously lots of people" in B.C. who don't know the Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a "quality individual" and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.
Why David Eby is considering a snap election
Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to "let politics go."
He said Clark and Campbell were among the "players" trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that "their time is over."

"That may mean time is over for me, too. I don't know," said Rustad. "But I'm not going to be trying to force my will or my vision in terms of what our party was … onto whoever the new leaders are going to be," he said.
"If they want me to be part of that in terms of supporting and building, I will do that. But it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside."
Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigns as leader of the B.C. Conservative Party
Rustad provides timeline

In a statement later Monday that confirmed he had accepted Doerkson's invitation, Rustad said talks between CentreBC and the Conservatives should succeed and the province "cannot afford two opposition parties" with an election looming.
Findlay's resignation followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, including the ejection of Rustad and two others on Friday.
He provided a timeline of the chaos the preceded that moment.
Rustad said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was "emotion and frustration around the table."
The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.
But on Friday he was told he was out.

Speculation about a snap election being called, less than two years since the 2024 election, intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham won't be running for a sixth term.
"After 17 years as the MLA for Saanich South, I have made the difficult decision not to seek re-election,” she said in a statement.
The minister of agriculture said her decision not to run again was difficult and sad.

Popham's statement came after NDP MLAs met Sunday night to discuss Findlay's departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.
"I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the B.C. Conservatives," the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

items: Snap election speculation grows as agriculture minister announces she won't run for 6th term
Lorne Doerkson named B.C. Conservatives interim leader following Findlay resignation

blocks.text: It went on to say the meeting was to "to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team," an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Premier David Eby's former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.
The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.
Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be "election ready."
McInnis releases statement
McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay's leadership.
Unlike other colleagues dissatisfied with Findlay, McInnis did not join CentreBC under their leader Peter Milobar.
McInnis said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return "home" came at a critical time for the province.
He rejected the need for "ideological purity tests" and said the prospect of a provincial election made a united opposition more important than ever.
No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a "big tent party," he said.

McInnis said he never lost respect for his Conservative caucus colleagues, with whom he shared a "common belief that British Columbians deserve practical solutions, fiscal resposiblity, and a government focused on delivering results."
Turmoil in the Conservative ranks, who have been divided over ideology and direction, birthed the CentreBC party which picked up eight legislators last week, including Milobar.
All are former Conservatives, including seven who quit that party's caucus in recent weeks, while Eleanor Sturko was ejected by Rustad last year.

The legislature still says the party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 24 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 18 Independents, including those joining CentreBC, Rustad and McInnis. Those numbers have not been updated since Sunday.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo-Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the B.C. Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before crossing the floor to join the Conservatives and being reelected in 2024.

articles.title: AfD makes gains in state elections, but has no government options
articles.summary: Despite making significant gains in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the far-right AfD remains without options to form a state government.

image.caption: AfD co-leader Alice Weidel (m) was jubilant following her party's good showing in state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western PomeraniaImage: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP

blocks.text: The Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in the elections in northeastern Germany and in the capital, Berlin, but is likely to remain in the opposition in both states.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) scored another election victory on Sunday evening, becoming the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania with 37.9% of the vote, according to an exit poll by the polling firm infratest-dimap on election night.

That put the far-right party just ahead of the Social Democrats (SPD), whose dramatic comeback in the last few weeks, led by incumbent State Premier Manuela Schwesig, fell just short, with 35.7% of the vote on Sunday evening. The final results may vary as votes are counted.

The AfD was not short of confidence. Even before the first exit poll results were announced, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla told public TV network ARD, "We clearly have a mandate to govern here," before adding that the party would offer coalition talks to all the other parties.
Chrupalla also said he expected Chancellor Friedrich Merz to resign now. "That would truly be a relief for this country," he said.

The AfD also made gains in the Berlin House of Representatives — the state parliament of the German capital — but fell far short of its own expectations on election night. According to infratest-dimap, it took 16.2% of the vote, though it had been polling at 18% only last week.
AfD: 'We are the new people's party!'
With Merz's center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) suffering heavy losses in both state elections, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel said she now sees her party as the successor to the CDU.

"We are the new people's party in Germany," Weidel pronounced to public broadcaster ZDF, before criticizing the Christian Democrats for refusing to entertain the possibility of entering into a coalition with AfD: "We are holding talks because we haven't erected any firewalls." But Weidel did not explain what the policy talks with other parties would look like.

After the AfD's triumph in the state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6, it has become clear that the party — some of whose members are considered a threat to Germany's constitutional order by German domestic intelligence agencies — is struggling to find political allies.

In that election, the AfD narrowly missed securing an absolute majority of seats in the state parliament and thus cannot elect the state premier on its own. In the struggle to form a governing majority, no party currently appears willing to enter into a coalition with the AfD.
No majorities for the AfD

However, the AfD's leading candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, had made it clear that he would only lead a "stable" AfD government, ruling out a minority government tolerated by representatives from other parties. During the election campaign, he had gone even further, repeatedly stating that he would only serve as state premier in a single-party AfD government.

Since then, it has been unclear exactly what the AfD is aiming for. The AfD's national leadership appears to have a strong interest in seeing form any kind of government. This was underscored by Weidel, who said after the elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania that the AfD could take power "even in a minority government."

Weidel herself is said to have ambitions to succeed Merz as chancellor. She was already her party's chancellor candidate in the last federal election in 2025, and many top AfD officials also see her as the chancellor candidate next time round. A successfully formed AfD state government could potentially give those ambitions a boost.

However, the party's rise has also been accompanied by growing protests. In the elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it was evident that many voters mobilized to keep the AfD's votes in check.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
AfD scandals during the campaign

The party also made several negative headlines during the election campaigns: In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, one AfD candidate had to pull out of the race when it emerged that he was a convicted bank robber. Another candidate withdrew his candidacy for the state parliament when it was revealed he had a DUI conviction and could no longer hold a driver's license.
In Berlin, meanwhile, drugs and Nazi memorabilia were found in the possession of a staff member of the party's lead candidate.

In the past, AfD politicians have repeatedly drawn criticism for making positive allusions to the Nazi era. One AfD European Parliament member posed with his hand on his heart in front of Adolf Hitler's "Führer Bunker" in Berlin, while one Bundestag member described himself as the "friendly face of National Socialism."
The influential AfD state leader in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, was twice fined for using a slogan of the notorious Sturmabteilung (SA), the paramilitary organization of Adolf Hitler's NSDAP party.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Germany faces energy tax losses as EV sales rise
articles.summary: The rapid shift to electric vehicles in Germany is cutting fuel tax revenue for the government. As EV sales surge, policymakers face growing pressure to find new ways to fund roads and transportation…

image.caption: Germany's shift to EVs is reducing emissions but eroding fuel tax revenues, raising questions about future transportation fundingImage: DW

blocks.text: "People are moving away from gasoline and diesel," Jens Boysen-Hogrefe, a tax and transportation expert at the Kiel Institute for the World Economy (IfW), told DW bluntly. "The boom in electric cars triggered by high fuel prices is accelerating the transition in drive technologies that was already planned anyway."
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), sales of electric vehicles in Europe rose by nearly 30% in the first quarter of 2025 compared with the same period last year.
Norway is leading the way, with electric cars accounting for as many as 95% of all newly registered cars in the country.

The agency's "Global EV Outlook 2026" reveals that EV growth rates in Asia-Pacific countries, excluding China, were even more remarkable, with sales in some regions rising by up to 80%. In Latin America, that figure was about 75%.
Fossil fuels remain a tax windfall
The boom in electric mobility has not been met with universal enthusiasm in the German government, as charging an electric car does not incur energy taxes, but only minimal electricity taxes.

Currently, a liter of diesel in Germany is taxed at 47.04 euro-cents (54 US cents per gallon), and a liter of gasoline at 65.45 euro-cents. On top of that, there is a carbon levy and a 19% value-added tax.
With gasoline priced at €2.10 per liter, taxes account for €1.14 of the total, meaning that more than half of the pump price goes to the government, according to the ADAC motoring club.

The current fossil-fuel-based system, with its energy taxes, truck tolls and CO2 tax, is very lucrative for the government, Boysen-Hogrefe said. "The finance minister doesn't benefit much when people drive electric cars," he noted. "Quite the opposite."
Energy tax revenue in decline

"If the shift to electric cars takes place and nothing changes in the tax system, the road system will become a money-losing venture for the federal government," Boysen-Hogrefe said, predicting billions of euros in losses.
EU overturns combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, revenue from the energy tax on diesel and gasoline fell from €37 billion in 2016 to €33 billion last year.
In 2022, a report by the scientific advisory committee to the German Transport Ministry projected that revenue from the energy tax would drop to as low as €5 billion by 2050.
Pressure to reform road funding

"The transition to electric vehicles has fiscal implications that have hardly been discussed so far," the report stated. The expected tax shortfalls add to the costly subsidies for electric vehicles that are currently still necessary to drive the transition forward, the report added.
In Germany, government incentives to purchase electric cars — amounting to several thousand euros per vehicle — were scrapped at the end of 2023.
Electric cars are still exempt from vehicle tax through 2035. And companies that invest in electric cars continue to enjoy tax benefits.
In their report, the transportation experts advised the government not to wait until the tax deficit becomes so large that it is forced to act.
That's because "the lead time for such measures spans several legislative terms," they argued.
Boysen-Hogrefe said fiscal pressure could now increase. If people continue to buy electric cars in droves, "the government can't just shrug it off," he said.
How other countries are responding
Countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have already come up with measures to deal with the new situation.

In the UK, a levy on electric cars is set to take effect in April 2028. The so-called "Electric Vehicle Excise Duty" charges 3 pence (3.5 euro-cents) per mile (1.6 kilometers) on fully electric cars and 1.5 pence on plug-in hybrids.
Since 2024, New Zealand and Iceland have required annual odometer checks for electric vehicles to calculate mileage-based fees.

In Switzerland, meanwhile, electric vehicle owners will be required to pay a road-use charge from 2030, either through a weight-based fee per kilometer or a tax on electricity purchased at charging stations.

Meanwhile, Norway, a trailblazer for electric vehicles, has restricted the VAT exemption for electric cars starting this year. It has also introduced a weight-based purchase or registration tax and tolls.
Why big automakers are losing China
Are road tolls the answer?
In Germany, many experts are advocating for a passenger car toll to compensate for the shortfall in energy tax revenue while also taking road use more fully into account.
"The recommended policy option is a distance- and traffic-based toll," according to a recently published study by the University of Münster.
"If we realistically assume that policymakers will shy away from this step, the vignette solution is recommended," according to the report.
Under a vignette system, drivers pay a flat fee for road use over a defined period.
"If this, too, encounters insurmountable political resistance, the only solution left is to raise the motor vehicle tax," they concluded.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development
articles.summary:
Beijing believes slowdown calls aim to lock in US advantage, and is pursuing a different balance between safety and pace

About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he…

blocks.text: About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
In response, he started developing his own AI study tool, concluding: “If you can’t beat them, join them.”
The pace and quality of AI development in China is second only to the United States, with the two superpowers locked in an intensifying rivalry as the stakes rise with each new model’s capabilities.
Analysts generally agree that frontier, or cutting-edge, US models are still some way ahead of their Chinese counterparts.

But over the last few weeks the mood music from Silicon Valley has been decidedly sombre, as insider after insider has warned of the potential catastrophes that could result from “loss of control” of the most advanced AIs.
And last Saturday Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched a “worldwide pacing of the frontier” – something he said would “require cooperation with China”.
“China is definitely not receptive” to a slowdown on US firms’ terms, though, said Lian Jye Su from technology research group Omdia.
For the government, AI is a “core sovereignty capability”, and Beijing will not want to jeopardise the progress made in closing the gap with US frontier models.
“It sees these calls [for a slowdown] as a bid to lock in US advantage,” said Su.
Amodei made this explicit, mentioning China specifically when arguing it was key “to keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.
He advocated for measures including continued export controls to China on advanced chips and machinery – the existence of which some argue already amounts to a forced unilateral “pacing”.
China’s foreign ministry responded to Amodei’s piece by saying “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance”.
However, several analysts told the Guardian it would be a mistake to assume this suggested a rejection of the broader concerns raised by the essay.

This week China released the third iteration of its AI safety governance framework – a document that functions as a “mapping of the AI risk landscape and roughly what one should do about it”, said Gabriel Wagner, a researcher at Concordia, a Beijing-based AI safety consultancy.

Included in the updates are the risks posed by agents, the cybersecurity threats from frontier models and the issue of recursive self-improvement – an as-yet hypothetical scenario where AI becomes advanced enough to improve itself.
“In many ways, I think there is more common ground than people might assume between what Amodei is saying and what the Chinese government is saying,” said Wagner.
That contrasts with US president Donald Trump, who this week called fears AI could wipe out humanity a “hoax”.
Trump is set to meet counterpart Xi Jinping in Washington next week, with AI expected to make the agenda, though analysts are sceptical a major breakthrough will happen.
The ruling Communist party, finely attuned to risks to its political control, has been proactive in ensuring the new technology has developed within boundaries set by the state.
Centralised authority over critical infrastructure and commercial activity means China is generally better placed than the United States “to address any AI disaster”, said Omdia’s Su.
However, Chinese companies do less voluntary monitoring and evaluation work than US ones, said Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (CEIP).
Neither government seems prepared for a loss-of-control incident like those outlined over the last few weeks, she said.
China’s regulation, though, is “iterative … they are quick to adapt and release new measures”, she added.
China has had an algorithm registry since 2022, but warnings on agents released this year suggest a switch in focus “from controlling what AI says to controlling what it does”, per Concordia AI.
Beijing also issued national regulations this year aimed at curbing emotional dependency on companion AIs.
At the same time, AI is being actively encouraged across the economy to promote growth, enshrining this goal in its latest Five Year Plan.

Local governments are offering funding and low rents to companies to help achieve this – entrepreneur But was recently invited to pitch his company, Hampshire Education, to a small city three hours from Shanghai set on establishing a reputation as a tech hub.
Factories across the country’s huge manufacturing base are being encouraged to convert their processes into the AI era.

“Safety and controllability are certainly major concerns, and they are actively discussed,” said a spokesperson for Black Lake Technologies, an industrial agent platform that says it has worked with 40,000 factories globally.
“But in manufacturing, these concerns tend to be much more concrete and operational … what companies care most about is whether the AI is reliable.”
Daily life in China is already highly digitised, with traditionally less discourse around data privacy helping with widespread adoption.
For example, digital health service A-fu, which features AI chatbot versions of prominent doctors trained on real clinical studies, recently hit 150 million users.
“Most people treat AI as an already-useful everyday tool, not an abstract threat, so the practical attitude is to live with it,” said Ni Tao, founding editor of tech website yangtzeer.com.
“There is real anxiety about jobs and misinformation, but it coexists with a strong belief that China must master AI rather than slow down.”
